Issue Reading note
Two reporting bases that do not tie The audited segment note reports Packaging / Testing / EMS / Others. Management reports ATM (packaging + testing + direct material + others) versus EMS. In 2Q26, ATM-basis packaging revenue was NT$100,324m against consolidated packaging of NT$99,387m, and ATM plus EMS (NT$191,937m) exceeded consolidated net revenue (NT$191,064m).
FY2025 is stale as a description of the business Consolidated gross margin was 17.7% for FY2025 and 21.0% in 2Q26; ATM gross margin 23.5% and 27.3%; free cash flow −NT$22bn for the year and −NT$40.5bn in the first half of 2026 alone.
The two variables that set the outcome are in no filing Capacity utilization is named as the margin driver in fourteen places in the FY2025 20-F and quantified in none of them. Leading-edge advanced packaging revenue, the line that explains the growth, appears in no 20-F or 6-K. Both series exist only in earnings-call remarks and are labelled as such throughout.
FY2018 discontinuity ASE Technology Holding was formed on 2018-04-30 from ASE and SPIL. FY2016–FY2017 are ASE only and exclude SPIL; FY2018 is a stub combining eight months of ASEH and SPIL with four months of predecessor ASE. The ADS ratio changed from five ASE shares to two ASEH shares at the same date. FY2017-to-FY2018 growth is not organic, and per-share series spanning April 2018 require the restated share counts.

The 20-F's US$ columns are convenience translations at a single period-end spot rate, so every series here is built in NT$ and translated once. Four NT$/US$ rates appear and each is named where it is used: NT$31.1 for FY2025 flows (the year's average), NT$31.4 for FY2025 year-end and 20-F convenience figures, NT$31.6 for 2Q26 flows (the quarter's average) and NT$32.47 for market values at 2026-08-03. Segment gross margin for packaging and testing has been reported as one combined figure since the FY2024 20-F, so no separate packaging or testing gross margin exists for FY2024 or FY2025. Peer financials for the six OSAT competitors that file nothing with the SEC (Powertech, King Yuan, JCET, Tongfu, Tianshui Huatian, ChipMOS on a TWSE basis) rest on third-party aggregators and trade press in the competitive sections.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

ASE sells the back end of the semiconductor supply chain. Customers or their foundries ship finished wafers to ASE on consignment, ASE turns them into packaged, tested parts, and ships them onward.▪ It never owns the silicon: "the cost of the silicon die, typically the most costly component of the packaged semiconductor, is usually not reflected in our costs (or revenues) since it is generally supplied by our customers on a consignment basis" (20-F FY2025, Item 5). Alongside that sits USI, a contract electronics manufacturer that buys components, assembles boards and modules, and sells the finished box.

Segment FY2023 FY2024 FY2025 % of FY2025 YoY FY24 YoY FY25
Packaging 256,806 261,731 308,343 47.8% +2% +18%
Testing 49,880 54,561 71,900 11.1% +9% +32%
EMS 268,218 271,293 257,193 39.9% +1% −5%
Others 7,011 7,823 7,952 1.2% +12% +2%
Total 581,914 595,410 645,388 100.0% +2% +8%

External revenue, NT$ millions, audited segment note (20-F FY2025, Note 41). "Others" holds in-house IC-substrate production and real-estate development and leasing, and recorded a pre-tax loss of NT$2,516m in FY2025.

What sets price: all three businesses are priced the same way and the disclosure is short: "We price our packaging services and EMS by considering the actual costs and prevailing market prices… Prices for our packaging, testing, and EMS are confirmed at the time orders are received from customers, which is typically several weeks before delivery" (20-F FY2025, Item 4.B). Testing adds a metering rule: price is set "primarily on the basis of the amount of time, measured in central processing unit seconds, taken by the automated testing equipment to execute the test programs specific to the products being tested, as well as the cost of the equipment." There is no disclosed contract duration, no escalator, no take-or-pay, no minimum volume and no backlog anywhere in ten years of 20-Fs.▪ The long-term service agreements that existed in 2021–22 were run down by 1Q23. Cost-plus pricing weeks before delivery means realized price is set by whoever has idle capacity, which is why the 20-F's standing description of the pricing regime is "a general trend toward declining prices for products and services of a given technology over time."

That regime has loosened. Management describes the current environment as "a very, very kind of a friendly pricing environment… we can definitely pass on these cost increases to our customers through our pricing arrangements" (Q2 2026 call, 2026-07-30). Blended factory utilization moved from roughly 65% expected for 1Q25 to 80–85% in 2Q26, and management's own published mapping puts 70% utilization at a 24% ATM gross margin and about 85% at 30% (UBS fireside, 2025-12-03).▪ ATM gross margin was 27.3% in 2Q26, close to where that curve predicts before any mix effect.

Who pays: one customer accounted for NT$161,282,046 thousand of FY2025 operating revenues, 25.0% of the group, spanning the packaging and EMS segments and including OEMs manufacturing on its behalf▪. It is named nowhere in any filing or transcript in the archive, and its revenue declined 7.6% in FY2025 while packaging revenue rose 17.8%. Top-five customers were 46.5% of FY2025 revenue, down from 48.4%. The group figure improved only because EMS shrank: on the ATM basis, top-five concentration rose from 41% (3Q25 and 4Q25) to 44% (2Q26) and top-ten from 58% to 60%, and the 4Q25 release named two customers each above 10% of ATM revenue. IDMs were 41% of 2Q26 ATM revenue, up from 38% in 1Q26.

Switching costs: customers qualify each ASE facility separately, a process the 20-F puts at "up to several weeks but can take longer," with an additional test correlation step of "up to two weeks." The 20-F also states plainly that "most of our customers obtain services from more than one source."▪

1.1 Packaging — 47.8% of revenue

Packaging revenue is disclosed only as a three-way product mix. Applying the disclosed percentages to the disclosed segment revenue gives the underlying lines:

Between FY2023 and FY2025 the segment added NT$51,537m of revenue and NT$52,031m of it came from the bump/flip-chip/WLP/SiP line; wirebonding subtracted NT$764m.▪

The one capacity unit ASE discloses is the installed wire bonder, and the filing says the industry uses it as the measure: "The number of bonders at a given facility is commonly used as a measure of the packaging capacity of the facility." The fleet peaked at 26,555 in the FY2020 report and has declined in every year since except 2022, to 24,815 at 2026-06-30.

The raw-material line is constrained two ways. Backing EMS material out of the group's disclosed NT$312,261m of raw material at the disclosed 78.7% EMS intensity, and allowing for testing consumables and the Others substrate operation, leaves 32.7% of packaging revenue. Backing the direct-material pass-through out of the 6-K's quarterly ATM raw-material disclosure gives 32.3–33.8% across three separate quarters. The two constructions span 32.3% to 33.8%.

Packaging raw-material intensity was 33.3% (FY2023), 31.6% (FY2024) and 32.7% (FY2025) while the advanced mix rose 8.3 percentage points. Amkor states the industry expectation directly: "We have expanded our business in advanced packaging, which tends to have higher material costs than our other products" (AMKR 10-K FY2025, Item 7). Either ASE's leading-edge work runs on customer- or foundry-supplied substrate the way wafers already arrive on consignment, or gold-to-copper wire conversion is cutting the wirebond base's intensity as fast as the advanced mix raises the blend. ASE discloses neither.

LEAP: "Leading-edge advanced packaging" is ASE's own label, defined by process rather than application: "We define leading-edge advanced packages as packaging technologies that incorporate redistribution layer (RDL) processes" (20-F FY2025, Item 4.B). Its revenue is disclosed only on earnings calls: US$250m in 2023, "over USD 600 million, accounting for around 6% of ATM revenues" in 2024, "$1.6 billion, accounting for 13% of ATM revenue" in 2025, guided above US$3.5bn for 2026 and "tracking ahead" of that, with management "aiming to double our LEAP revenue in 2027."▪ Within LEAP, 75% is assembly and 25% test; within test, 75% is wafer sort. Full-process work, meaning ASE's own end-to-end flow rather than discrete steps allocated out of a foundry partner's line, is guided at about 10% of LEAP revenue in 2026, up from about 3% in 2025. Converting at 75% assembly share gives LEAP packaging revenue of roughly NT$37,800m in FY2025, about 12.3% of packaging revenue [estimate: LEAP × 75% × NT$31.5/US$; a ±3% FX error moves this by ±NT$1.1bn].

FY2024→FY2025 packaging growth of NT$46,611m decomposes as roughly 50% LEAP assembly, 38% mainstream advanced packaging, 14% wirebonding and −2% discrete [estimate: §1.1 mix arithmetic].

Operating leverage: up-cycle incremental gross margins in this segment historically ran 39–50%. FY2025 delivered 25.6% at the gross line and 4.5% at the pre-tax line on NT$46,611m of extra revenue, the worst conversion of the decade in the year revenue grew fastest.▪ Management gave the mechanism in advance: "we see our depreciation rising faster than revenues as a result of our ongoing investments in LEAP… our LEAP lines must be installed at scale and together as a full set of differing machinery instead of small incremental units like wirebonders and testers" (Q1 2026 call). The first half of 2026 shows the reversal: ATM revenue rose from NT$179,233m (1H25) to NT$238,582m with gross margin moving 22.2% to 26.7%, an incremental gross margin of 40.2% and an incremental operating margin of 31.2%.▪

Capital intensity: packaging capex ran between 10.9% and 22.4% of segment revenue from FY2019 to FY2024 and reached 36.8% in FY2025, at 3.04x the segment's D&A and rental charge. Packaging D&A sat between NT$32.3bn and NT$34.4bn for six consecutive years on a revenue base that grew 32%, so the old asset base was generating revenue at near-zero incremental capital cost. That ended in FY2025. Cumulative FY2024–FY2025 packaging capex of NT$171,958m produced a revenue increment of NT$51,537m, NT$3.34 of capex per NT$1.00 of new annual revenue, against NT$1.18 in the FY2020–21 boom.

Testing sells machine time. Revenue equals installed testers times utilization times realized revenue per tester-year, and ASE discloses the first term only.▪

Segment gross margin cannot be reconciled and the reason is specific: ASE discloses gross margin only for ATM combined and for EMS, never for testing alone, and the audited segment note stops at profit before income tax. Test consumes almost no materials — Amkor states the industry fact, "Test materials constitute a very small portion of our total test cost" — so no supplier or customer disclosure bounds testing COGS independently.

The marginal machine costs roughly twice what the average installed machine cost and earns at most 1.77x as much.▪ Capital cost per net tester added reproduces at US$1.08m (FY2025), US$1.05m (2Q26) and US$1.14m (1H26); marginal revenue per incremental tester is US$591k a year against a fleet average of US$334k. Against a depreciable life implied at five to seven years but never disclosed, and management's own pre-tax discount rate of 11.96–13.81% for its goodwill test, the payback on the marginal machine is not obviously better than on the installed fleet.

FY2024→FY2025 testing growth of 31.8% splits almost exactly in half: average fleet +15.8%, revenue per tester +13.8%. The utilization lift alone, on management's disclosed bands, accounts for roughly +18%, so mix and price contributed close to nothing net of the fleet being newer and partly idle during installation [estimate: residual after the disclosed utilization band; wide because the utilization figures are ATM-blended, not test-specific].

Capital intensity here is the highest in the group. Segment capex was 71.8% of segment revenue in FY2025 against 36.8% for packaging and 2.3% for EMS, all three on external segment revenue. Test equipment capex by quarter went US$199m (3Q25), US$218m (4Q25), US$326m (1Q26), US$804m (2Q26), the last of which exceeds the segment's own quarterly revenue. Management's FY2026 plan puts 40% of US$6.5bn of equipment capex, roughly US$2.6bn, into test against FY2026 testing revenue of roughly US$3.16bn [estimate: 1H26 actual plus the guided 3Q26 and a normal 4Q26]. Cumulatively across FY2018–FY2025, the segment produced NT$24,494m of pre-tax cash after capex on NT$408,113m of revenue, a 6.0% conversion, and it turned cash-negative in FY2024.

1.3 EMS — 39.9% of revenue

Raw materials were 78.7% of EMS revenue in FY2025 and 79% in 2Q26, and the CFO confirmed component cost is passed straight through ("And so the memory is just sort of a pass-through type of cost for you guys?" / "That's correct.", Q2 2026 call). The reported revenue line is therefore roughly four-fifths a restatement of what USI bought from its suppliers, and the informative series is value-added revenue, meaning revenue less raw material.▪

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

ASE runs real technology. The differentiation is in test.

The architectures are shared. The FY2025 20-F defines the whole leading-edge category by process rather than by invention, and every architecture in its table has a shipping rival▪: FOCoS against TSMC CoWoS-S and Amkor S-SWIFT; FOCoS-Bridge against TSMC CoWoS-L, Intel EMIB, Amkor S-Connect and Samsung I-Cube-E; fan-out with embedded bridge dies also sold by Deca and IBM (marklapedus.substack.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. The redistribution-layer and solder-bumping foundations that define the category are partly licensed in, non-exclusively, from Infineon, TDK and DECA Technologies (20-F FY2025, Intellectual Property). ASE owns 17.82% of DECA and 18.74% of Chipletz, which mitigates the dependency without removing it.

Most of the leading-edge revenue is someone else's process flow. Reconstructing 2026 LEAP from management's own splits: roughly 66% is on-substrate work, meaning discrete back-end steps allocated out of a foundry partner's CoWoS flow; about 19% is wafer probe; under 10% is ASE's own architecture end to end; about 6% is final test▪ [estimate: management-disclosed percentage splits applied to the disclosed LEAP base; ASE publishes no such table]. Full-process work at roughly US$300m is about 1.8% of FY2026E ATM revenue. Dr. Tien Wu describes the boundary himself: "there are packaging that needs to be taken by the foundry people because access to the leading edge wafer is simply not available to the others… In terms of where do we stop the line, when do we start the line, that depends on the wisdom of the management team of the ecosystem collaborator" (Q2 2026 call).

The stated policy is fast-following. The head of investor relations put it plainly: "We like to do things when — we don't like to get very much ahead of the technology. I think those situations result in less than optimal returns for the overall company" (UBS fireside, 2025-12-03). That sits against the COO's claim on the 2Q26 call of "first mover advantages… technology, speed, capacity and most importantly, trust." The financial record supports the first description: ASE's own end-to-end leading-edge line was roughly 1–2% of ATM revenue in FY2025–26.▪

LEAP mechanics: a redistribution layer is a thin-film metal routing layer built on the die or on a reconstituted wafer or panel, fanning the die's pads out to a coarser pitch and routing die-to-die without going down into an organic substrate. It matters because an AI accelerator now integrates one to three logic dies with 8 to 16 HBM stacks, and NVIDIA's Rubin Ultra substrate is 153 × 77 mm with a 124 × 50 mm interposer (UBS fireside, 2025-12-03). Organic substrate cannot deliver die-to-die bandwidth at that pitch; a silicon interposer can but is expensive and reticle-limited. FOCoS mounts a fan-out module on a high pin-count BGA substrate and lets the RDL handle the short hops, at 3,000–7,000 leads. FOCoS-Bridge embeds silicon bridges in the fan-out RDL so only the highest-density hops use silicon, at 3,000–14,000 leads; the published TSV variant is an 85 × 85 mm test vehicle with two fan-out modules, each one ASIC plus four HBM3 stacks, using 3 RDLs at 5 µm line/space for 72% lower resistance and 50% lower inductance than the non-TSV version [web, marklapedus.substack.com].

What is hard: yield at 85–100 mm package size, warpage control across an organic substrate with large silicon content, sub-micron die-attach accuracy, RDL at 2 µm line/space, and the capital and building lead time to run it at scale. ASE is running 13 greenfield and 8 brownfield construction projects simultaneously — management gave both 8 and 7 for the brownfield count on the same call — and names buildings as a gating factor. Not hard enough to exclude anyone: TSMC has shipped CoWoS-S since 2012 and CoWoS-L since 2022, Intel shipped EMIB in 2017, Amkor sells S-SWIFT and S-Connect, Samsung Foundry sells I-Cube-E. Dr. Wu's own framing of durability is that the architecture layer is churn: "I have been working in the packaging industry for 40 years. I've gone through about 1,000 different packaging design. At the end of the day, probably 20 will leave."

Panel-level packaging: at a 100 × 100 mm package only about seven modules fit on a 300 mm wafer, and at five to six reticle sizes utilization drops to 57%; a rectangular panel raises that to about 87% (UBS fireside)▪. ASE's announced line uses 310 × 310 mm panels supporting 2/2 µm RDL for FOCoS (aseglobal.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. The scarce asset is automation rather than the panel: "Today, we already have manual. But in my view, the manual process doesn't count. I can only count in this space, it needs to be fully light out" (Q4 2025 call). TSMC's CoPoS targets the same 310 × 310 format with a pilot line in 2026 and mass production in 2H 2028, and Dr. Wu describes the two as "quite complementary. It's actually the same customer set, similar the reticle size. In terms of the pitch size line width, they're all identical." Identical specifications for the same customers describes a second source. The production date has moved twice in six months, from "by the end of this year" (Q4 2025 call) to first-half 2027 (press release, 2026-05-26) to "start production by Q1 of next year" (Q2 2026 call).

Co-packaged optics: converting the electrical interface to optical inside the package removes the copper resistive and length penalty. ASE has passive fibre alignment, laser-direct cavity formation, electronic-IC-on-photonic-IC stacking via fan-out package-on-package, and a demonstrated 75 × 75 mm network-IC test vehicle with eight fibre attachments. The revenue evidence is the point: "At this point, the silicon photonics revenue levels for us are still relatively small" (UBS fireside), and nine months later, "On the CPO, I would like to wait for 2 quarters before I give you more detail… By the way, we have been working on this for about 20 years" (Q2 2026 call). Twenty years of development has produced immaterial revenue.

Test is the under-exploited differentiator. The proprietary asset in test is not the tester, which Teradyne, Advantest and Tokyo Electron sell to everyone. It is multi-platform test-program conversion: "This portability between testers enables us to allocate semiconductors tested across our available test capabilities and thereby improve capacity utilization rates" (20-F FY2025). In a business where utilization is the entire margin, moving a device to whichever tester is free is worth more than any package architecture in the portfolio, and ASE has disclosed it in the same language for a decade.▪ The same capability cuts the other way: every conversion ASE performs reduces the platform-specificity that would otherwise lock a customer in.

The patent estate is not growing. Total patents held went 6,433 (2024-01-31) to 6,433 (2025-01-31) to 6,358 (2026-01-31), and pending applications from 2,351 to 2,249, while R&D expense rose 14.0% to NT$32,852m and R&D headcount reached 14,258.▪ Patent counts fall through expiry and abandonment. The estate did not grow in the years the LEAP platform was built, which is the period a patents-based advantage claim would have to rest on.

The substitution ASE does not discuss: hybrid bonding pulls the highest-value interconnect step into a fab-grade environment. Amkor names "copper hybrid bonding" as a development programme in its FY2025 10-K; the phrase appears nowhere in ASE's FY2023–FY2025 20-Fs or in 24 earnings calls.▪ Glass core substrate is the other watch item, and ASE's position is explicit: "we do not have the glass substrate in production, not for the next 12 months" (Q2 2026 call).

Roadmap exposure is low. On the 2026 base of more than US$3,500m, roughly 66% is on-substrate work already running, 25% is test already running, and under 10% is full process, which is qualified and ramping in 4Q26. Panel, co-packaged optics, power delivery and glass contribute nothing to 2026 and, on management's own comments, little to 2027. The 2027 doubling is a capacity and allocation commitment rather than a technology bet. Dr. Wu frames it that way: "the business demand is not a concern. It's our own capability to execute."

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

3.1 Packaging

The advantage is cost position and allocation priority, and it has not yet reached the capital line.▪ Against Amkor, the only other listed pure-play OSAT of comparable technology reach, ASE's assembly-and-test operations earned a 12.1% pre-tax margin in FY2025 against 6.6%, and a 23.5% gross margin against 14.0%.▪ That gap has been present every year since FY2019 and widened from 3.5 points to 5.5 points at the pre-tax line. It comes from things Amkor cannot buy quickly: 24,815 wire bonders, roughly a third of top-ten OSAT revenue, a Taiwan cluster co-located with the foundry that allocates the leading-edge work, and a preferred-provider alliance with TSMC dating to 1997.

None of it reaches the return on capital. Estimated packaging ROIC was 8.6% in FY2025 excluding working capital, against Amkor's 9.5% computed the same way, and the packaging figure was below Amkor's in four of the last five years once the SPIL merger goodwill is included.▪ ASE spent 36.8% of packaging revenue on capex in FY2025 and 3.0x its own depreciation, against Amkor's 13.5% of revenue. A 1.8x pre-tax margin advantage converts into no return advantage because roughly three times the capital is deployed per revenue dollar.

Segment assets have not been disclosed since FY2016, so every packaging return figure is an allocation of consolidated PP&E with a band of NT$233–278bn on net PP&E alone, worth roughly plus or minus 8 percentage points of ROIC at the extremes; the figures above use the capex-less-depreciation roll-forward. And FY2025 was the trough of an investment cycle. Annualising 2Q26 ATM operating profit of NT$19,782m and taxing it at the quarter's 16.4% effective rate gives NOPAT of about NT$66,150m on an ATM invested-capital base estimated near NT$460–500bn, a 13–14% run-rate against the 8.7% FY2025 figure [estimate: annualised quarter on an allocated capital base].

The pricing rule is disclosed: packaging is priced on "the actual costs and prevailing market prices," and management describes cost pass-through rather than premium pricing. When utilization dropped to roughly 60% in 2024, packaging's pre-tax margin was 11.1% and the estimated ROIC 10.5%. The margin follows the loading, which is what a capacity business does and what a business protected by network effects or switching costs does not.▪

Management claims: scale and specialisation give "greater efficiency at lower cost while maintaining equivalent or higher quality" than a captive IDM line; pure-play neutrality means "we have no conflict with foundry, with no conflict with substrate provider"; LEAP is accretive to structural margin. External sources: Amkor names ASE first among its competitors and ranks price seventh of eight competitive factors; ASE is estimated to receive the majority of TSMC's outsourced CoWoS work [web, low confidence]; ASE reportedly raised advanced-packaging quotes by more than 20% in mid-2026 (siliconanalysts.com citing TrendForce, accessed 2026-08-03) [web, unverified]; and UBS put it to management on 2025-12-03 that ASE's CoWoS/FOCoS ramp came "a bit later than some of your peers," which drew no rebuttal. Ground-up view: in a capacity industry with cost-plus pricing, concentrated buyers and a scarce input controlled upstream, excess returns accrue only while capacity is short, and then to whoever has the lowest unit cost and the best allocation position. ASE has the second and is currently enjoying the first.

Excess returns today at the top of the cycle, defensible for now, open to erosion as rivals, customers and the foundry partner shift.▪ There is no self-reinforcing loop and the returns collapse with loading. Packaging out-margins every listed OSAT peer and has done so through a full cycle.

Business-model analogues: Lonza is the closest public reference class: a biologics contract manufacturer selling qualified capacity for a customer-owned molecule, where site-and-process qualification is the switching cost, scale is the cost advantage, utilization is the whole margin story and capex is committed years ahead of revenue. It breaks where Lonza's qualification is enforced by a regulator and takes years to move, while a package qualification takes weeks. Jabil is the second: anchor-customer contract manufacturing at scale where the customer's allocation decision sets the growth rate; it breaks because ASE's process R&D at 6.7% of ATM revenue and its margins are roughly three times Jabil's. Amkor is the same business at one-third the scale, with materially lower margins and the same return on capital. TSMC is not an analogue despite the sector: it sets price, earned a 59.9% gross margin in FY2025, and is simultaneously ASE's partner and its named competitor.

3.2 Testing

Testing earns excess returns only at the top of the cycle, and the evidence does not support a durable structural advantage.▪

The adjacency is physical. ASE is the largest packager in the world, wafers arrive on consignment for assembly, and the test steps beside the assembly flow — wafer probing and drop shipment — attach almost mechanically. That shows in the numbers: wafer probing rose from 35.4% of testing revenue in FY2023 to 44.0% in FY2025 while final testing declined from 61.5% to 54.0%.

None of the four things a durable moat would require is present. Scale does not show up as a cost or margin advantage: ASE's testing segment is roughly 2.1x King Yuan Electronics by revenue and earns a lower operating margin, 22.2% of gross segment revenue in FY2025 against 25.8%, and the gap has moved 8.3 points against ASE since FY2021.▪ Switching costs are weeks, and ASE's own test-program conversion capability exists specifically to make programs portable across tester platforms. There is no IP position: the 6,358 patents are described as related to packaging technologies, and the testers are bought at market prices from Teradyne, Tokyo Electron and Advantest, with part of the fleet consigned by customers and "dedicated exclusively to the testing of these customers' specific products" and part leased. Pricing is explicitly cost-plus on CPU-seconds and equipment cost, "with additional consideration of prevailing market prices," and the 20-F states that average selling prices "have experienced sharp declines" when competitors chase utilization.

The downcycle behaviour is the hardest counter-evidence to the scale claim. In FY2023 King Yuan's revenue declined 34.8% and its operating margin declined 3.0 points; ASE Testing's revenue declined 10.9% and its operating margin declined 6.9 points. The larger, better-diversified, utilization-managed fleet showed materially worse operating leverage on a far smaller volume decline.

The returns confirm the structure. FY2025 testing ROIC is an estimated 10.3%, range 9.1–11.4%, against an NT$-denominated cost of capital of roughly 8–9%, and ROIIC since FY2019 is an estimated 8.0–9.8% [estimate: net PP&E near NT$100,000m, from an accounting roll-forward off the FY2016 segment-asset disclosure and from a depreciation-implied net book value; the two span NT$95,000–105,000m]. King Yuan, on a third-party computation of its own filings, earns 11.2% ROIC on one-half the revenue. Over FY2017–FY2025 the segment produced NT$224,356m of pre-tax EBITDA and spent NT$190,990m of capital expenditure: 85 cents of every EBITDA dollar went back into equipment.

The attach thesis fails where the AI test work actually landed. Trade coverage attributes the dominant position in NVIDIA final test, system-level test and burn-in to King Yuan, though neither company names the other (datacenterdynamics.com and trendforce.com, both accessed 2026-08-03) [web, low confidence]. ASE's own disclosure is consistent with a wafer-sort-first position: leading-edge test is 25% of LEAP revenue and 75% of that is wafer sort, so AI final test is roughly 6% of LEAP. Management has prioritized wafer sort over final test in four consecutive appearances while stating that it is building final-test capacity and expects "meaningful revenue being generated in the later part of next year." ASE did not win the final-test and burn-in insertions on AI accelerators.▪

Analogues: Amkor is the same business built the same way at similar strength. GlobalFoundries is the closer structural analogue for the returns profile — qualified-into-the-customer's-flow capacity, real but bounded switching costs, ROIC hovering near the cost of capital — and it breaks because GlobalFoundries has multi-year single-source agreements with customer prepayments and ASE's test business has none. The reference class ASE Testing does not belong to, and is sometimes credited with, is co-located capacity protected by contract or regulation: Linde's on-site industrial-gas plants with 15–20-year take-or-pay inside the customer's fence, or Lonza's regulated capacity where requalification runs years. Those share the adjacency logic and add the legal lock ASE lacks.

3.3 EMS

EMS has no durable competitive advantage. It earns approximately its cost of capital, it does not set price, and its position relative to the four US-listed contract manufacturers has deteriorated over five years.▪

It does not set price. In July 2026 the CFO guided third-quarter EMS revenue up "around 40% quarter-over-quarter," attributed the increase to memory component price inflation, confirmed under direct questioning that memory is "a pass-through type of cost," and put the same quarter's operating margin ex-price-hikes at "around 3.7%, 3.8%" against reported guidance of 3.2%–3.4%. Revenue can inflate 40% in a quarter on input prices while profit dollars barely move, and the reported margin gets worse as those prices rise.

Returns are at the cost of capital on two computations. Building invested capital from the balance sheet of USI Shanghai — the 71.6%-held SSE-listed vehicle whose FY2025 revenue of RMB 59,195m converts to roughly NT$257.5bn against ASE's disclosed EMS external revenue of NT$257,193m — gives invested capital of 22.6% of revenue and a ROIC of 10.2%, range 8.8%–12.7% [estimate]. USI Shanghai's own audited weighted-average return on equity filed with the Shanghai Stock Exchange was 9.98% (2025), 9.52% (2024) and 12.02% (2023) [web]. USI Shanghai is consolidated into the EMS segment, so these are not independent observations; they are computed from different statements and span 9.98% to 10.2%. ASE's own goodwill impairment testing applied pre-tax discount rates of 11.96%–13.81% in 2025, roughly 9%–11% after tax.

In FY2020 ASE's EMS unit had the highest gross margin and the highest operating margin of this five-company set. In FY2025 it has the lowest operating margin.▪ Every US-listed peer expanded gross margin by 100–445bp over the same five years; ASE's EMS gross margin is where it started. Of the three that report a June-2026 quarter it has the lowest gross margin (8.9%), the lowest operating margin (2.4%) and the slowest growth (+11.9%); Jabil and Flex are not in that comparison.

Operating expense explains the whole deficit. Gross margin of 9.15% sits in the middle of the peer range of 8.81%–12.06%; the operating expense ratio of 6.20% is 130–250bp above every peer, driven by R&D at 2.62% of revenue against Jabil's 0.09% and Celestica's 0.95%. Closing the opex gap to the peer median of about 4.4% would add roughly 180bp of operating margin, about NT$4.7bn on FY2025 revenue, which is 61% more than the segment actually earned.

A qualification switching cost survives its evidence test, weakly. Twelve country sites hold IATF 16949, ISO 13485, ISO 26262, TISAX, AS/EN 9100 and TL 9000 approvals, and USI's Nantou facility is qualified by the US Defense Logistics Agency. That produces stickiness at the programme level, and consumer electronics, 35.7% of FY2025 EMS revenue, turns over in 12–24 months. Returns are at or barely above the cost of capital, with price-taking and commodity-like competition.

Analogues: Flex and Sanmina are built the same way and are modestly stronger, both earning roughly 16% ROIC against ASE EMS's ~10%. Jabil is the same shape but structurally better positioned on capital: it runs negative operating working capital of −US$1,335m at FY2025 year end, so its customers fund it, and its invested capital is 8.8% of revenue against 22.6% at ASE's EMS. Outside electronics, Magna is the nearest analogue by moat shape — design-and-build to a customer's specification, programme-qualified, tooling tied to a customer's product cycle — and it breaks because automotive programme life is five to seven years against 12–24 months in consumer electronics, which makes ASE's EMS the less sticky of the two.

3.4 Returns: standalone, versus peers, over time

Standalone, ten years: consolidated gross margin ranged 15.6% (FY2019) to 20.1% (FY2022) and was 17.7% in FY2025. Operating margin ranged 5.6% to 12.1% and was 8.0%. ROIC peaked at 15.0% in FY2022 and was 8.2% in FY2025, below 10% in seven of the nine years it can be computed. Free-cash-flow margin was negative for the first time in FY2025, at −3.5%.

ROIC = NOPAT divided by average invested capital, where NOPAT = operating income times (1 − effective tax rate) and invested capital = total debt plus total equity including non-controlling interests less cash and cash equivalents. ROIIC = the change in NOPAT divided by the change in invested capital over the stated window.

The window changes the answer. From the FY2022 cycle peak to FY2025 it is −25.1%: NOPAT declined NT$22.9bn while invested capital rose NT$91bn. From the FY2023 trough to FY2025 it is +4.2%. From FY2019 to FY2025, one full cycle and the fair window for a cyclical, it is +14.0%. A cost of capital for a Taiwan-listed manufacturer with NT$261bn of debt at 6.9x interest coverage is not materially below 8%, so FY2025 returns sit approximately at break-even on that basis and only FY2021–FY2022 cleared it convincingly.

Every player in the chain is inflecting on the same industry-wide rise in utilization. ASE's ATM-versus-Amkor gross-margin gap went from 9.5pp on FY2025 to 10.5pp in 2Q26 and the operating-margin gap from 4.3pp to 5.2pp: no erosion, and no dramatic widening either. Amkor is participating at a similar rate of improvement, which is what happens when the driver is industry loading rather than a company-specific edge.▪

Over time: the margin gap versus Amkor widened against FY2019–20 and has been flat since FY2022. The ROIC gap has never turned durably positive: −7.8pp (FY2021), −6.2pp (FY2022), −0.3pp (FY2023), +0.4pp (FY2024), −0.9pp (FY2025). In test, the operating-margin gap versus King Yuan went from +4.7pp in ASE's favour (FY2021) to −3.6pp against it (FY2025), an 8.3-point swing. Both statements are true at once and the reconciliation is capital intensity.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

4.1 Market structure and the share number that circulates

TrendForce's widely-syndicated 2024 top-ten OSAT ranking puts ASE first at US$18.54bn with "nearly a 45% share among the top ten" of a US$41.56bn pool (trendforce.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. That US$18.54bn is ASEH's entire consolidated revenue: NT$595,410m divided by 32.1 gives US$18.55bn, a match to within 0.05%. It includes roughly US$8.4bn of USI contract-electronics revenue at an 8.9% gross margin that does no semiconductor packaging at all, while every other player in the table is measured on OSAT revenue only.▪

The correction does not change who is first; it changes the structure from "one dominant player at 45% plus a long tail" to a leader near 32%, a credible number two near 18% and a Chinese number three near 14%.▪ Top-three is 64.4% of the top-ten and the HHI within that universe is 1,792; scaling for a tail of small and regional OSATs at 15–25% of the total market gives an HHI of roughly 1,000–1,300, moderately concentrated, and an ASE share of 24–27% of all outsourced assembly and test.

The share that moved in 2025 moved from Amkor to ASE, not from China to ASE. JCET, Tongfu and Tianshui Huatian went from 31.2% of top-ten revenue in 2024 to 31.2% in 2025, growing 13.7% in aggregate against a market that grew 13.6%. ASE grew 20.7%; Amkor grew 6.2%.▪ The China threat in packaging is real at the mature and commodity end and in domestic substitution. It did not cost ASE share in 2025.

Nobody in this industry sets price.▪ The 20-F says why: average selling prices decline over a technology's life and decline faster "during periods of intense competition… as a result of intense price competition from other market participants that attempt to maintain high-capacity utilization levels in the face of reduced demand." The marginal supplier with idle capacity sets the price. The 2026 exception is management's own framing: "we're expecting a favorable pricing environment for the year," qualified by "The price hike is not part of the structure margin… the price hike is a very opportunistic approach."

ASE is the scale leader on total outsourced packaging revenue, at 1.8–1.9x Amkor's packaging-only revenue and roughly 2x JCET's▪; on wire-bond capacity, where no competitor discloses a comparable fleet and ASE's FY2025 wire-bond revenue of US$3.23bn is 2.8x Amkor's entire mainstream line; and on turnkey breadth. It is roughly at parity on the broad advanced-package line, where its US$5.85bn compares with Amkor's US$5,556m of Advanced Products, a figure that includes the related test revenue ASE books in a separate segment. It trails at the leading edge: US$1.6bn of FY2025 LEAP against TSMC's advanced packaging at roughly 8–10% of FY2025 revenue, about US$10–13bn [estimate: TSMC's CFO put advanced packaging at about 8% of revenue on the 4Q25 call; other coverage puts it slightly above 10%]. Any statement that ASE leads advanced packaging is false unless explicitly scoped to the merchant layer.▪

The competitor closing fastest is Amkor, on capital commitment rather than revenue. It went from 13.5% capex intensity in FY2025 to a FY2026 plan of US$2.5–3.0bn, roughly 40% of revenue, including a US$7bn Arizona campus [web]. That converges Amkor's capital intensity toward ASE's for the first time in a decade, and on Amkor's own timeline it does not convert to revenue before 2029.

The disclosed independent-test pool sums to NT$162,761m, US$5,225m at the FY2025 average rate of NT$31.1, across six players, an HHI of 2,750 with ASE contributing 1,954 of it. The pool covers only players that disclose a test line, so it excludes Amkor, which has not split packaging from test in any 10-K since at least FY2013; foundry in-house probe, which TSMC never sizes; the Chinese OSATs, which disclose no test line; and IDM captive test. On a global basis ASE's share of outsourced test is 26–33% [estimate: disclosed pool grossed up for Amkor at the mid-point of a US$1.27–1.61bn band plus US$0.8–1.0bn for China OSAT and other Asian test houses].

Taiwan's IC-test industry produced roughly NT$211bn of output value, derived two ways: TSIA/ITRI data quoted in King Yuan's 2024 annual report puts 4Q24 at NT$52.8bn, and Taiwan's 2025 IC packaging-and-testing projection of NT$673bn less IC packaging of NT$461.5bn leaves NT$211.5bn [web]. The first annualises a quarter that was itself declining both sequentially and year over year, and the two derivations span NT$211.0–211.5bn. ASE Testing's NT$71,900m is 34.0% of that as an upper bound, or 22–34% adjusting for ASE's non-Taiwan test sites [estimate: Taiwan headcount share of 64% as the lower-bound weighting].

The largest quantified opportunity in the segment, and the counter-evidence to it: ASE's test-to-packaging revenue ratio was 0.233x in FY2025. Management states the structural target on the record: "A more natural percentage is probably closer to maybe a 30% or 1/3, 2/3 type relationship between testing and assembly. So we do have quite a bit of growth opportunity if we just test the products that we package" (UBS fireside, 2025-12-03). At a 0.5x ratio on FY2025 packaging revenue, the un-attached pool is NT$82,271m, US$2.64bn at the FY2025 average rate [estimate: management's stated ratio applied to disclosed packaging revenue], which is 2.4x King Yuan's entire FY2025 revenue. Against that, the FY2025 segment note discloses that the single customer at 25.0% of group revenue buys from "packaging and EMS segments," not testing. The 25%-of-revenue customer does not buy ASE's test services at a material level.▪ The only >10% turnkey test customer ASE ever disclosed, "customer B" at NT$44,653,072 thousand of FY2019 revenue, disappeared after US export controls took effect in September 2020, and the tester count went from 5,767 (Jan-2021) to 4,918 (Jan-2022) as ASE rebalanced.

4.5 Share counter-evidence

  • Foundry forward-integration. TSMC is simultaneously ASE's strategic ally since 1997, its source of consigned wafers, and, in ASE's own words, an advanced-packaging competitor via InFO. TSMC's advanced-packaging revenue is comparable in size to ASE's entire ATM business. The competition risk factor has stated since FY2021 that "some foundry players have actively invested and expanded their advanced packaging capacity and gained some customer bases with their services and solutions." ASE's fastest-growing business is served at the allocation of a partner that is also the largest competitor in that business.▪
  • Amkor's capital step-up and the US onshoring premium. Amkor's FY2026 capex of US$2.5–3.0bn plus a US$7bn Arizona campus, and King Yuan's announced US operation, both target the geography ASE has explicitly declined to build in first. Asked directly on 2026-07-30, Dr. Wu said ASE will "develop and build fully automated efficient line in Taiwan… In due time, we will migrate and move the operation to the other places in the world." If US customers begin requiring domestic advanced packaging, Taiwan-first sequencing is a share risk in the 2028–2030 window.
  • Chinese domestic substitution at the mature end. Not a 2025 share event, but Tongfu grew 16.9% and Huatian 19.0% on domestic demand and state support. ASE's exposure runs through the wirebonding line at 32.9% of packaging revenue and the discrete line, the segments a China-for-China supply chain substitutes most easily. Amkor names the mechanism: "geopolitical trade tensions have increased competition from Chinese firms supporting a China-for-China supply chain."
  • King Yuan's capital escalation in AI final test. NT$50bn of 2026 capex against NT$34.9bn of FY2025 revenue, plus customer-consigned tools that add capacity without consuming its own balance sheet. ASE has said it will not contest this until late 2026.
  • Customer concentration, running the other way. A single sourcing decision by the 25%-of-revenue customer moves more of the packaging segment than any competitor's capacity addition would.
  • IDM re-insourcing, which runs ASE's way. IDMs were 41% of 2Q26 ATM revenue and ASE keeps buying their captive sites: Motorola's, ISE Labs, EEMS Test Singapore, Infineon's Philippines and South Korea subsidiaries in 2024, and a March 2026 board resolution on Analog Devices' Malaysia subsidiaries. These counterparties are customers and asset vendors at once.

5. Value chain and profit pools

ASE has the most leverage over throughput of any layer in the chain and captures the least of the end price. It converts a bare die worth thousands of dollars into a saleable part for a fee that is a low single-digit percentage of that part's selling price, and it does so without owning the die.▪

Gross margin across the chain is bimodal. Design and foundry earn 60–71%. The physical-conversion layers, substrate at 24.8% and OSAT at 27.3% and 16.8%, earn between a quarter and two-fifths of that.▪ The equipment layer earns 58% gross but only 20% operating, because it spends the difference on R&D. At the very top, a near-monopoly on a consumable film earns above a 50% operating margin on US$0.67bn of sales.

ASE and Unimicron are near-identical on both margin lines in 2Q26: gross margin 27.3% against 24.8%, operating margin 15.7% against 15.5%. The substrate maker and the packager earn the same return, which is evidence against substrate scarcity being extracted from ASE as a rent today.▪ The direction is another matter: Unimicron's gross margin rose 6.8 points sequentially in 2Q26 against ASE ATM's 1.3 points.

One AI accelerator's dollar: for an NVIDIA B200 at a US$30,000–40,000 selling price, Epoch AI's published Monte-Carlo build puts total manufacturing cost at about US$6,400 (range US$5,700–7,300), of which HBM3E is roughly US$2,880–3,264 and advanced packaging about US$1,100 (range US$1,000–1,200), with no separate test line (epoch.ai, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. That puts the packaging step at 2.8–3.7% of the chip's selling price. A top-down cross-check from TSMC's own disclosure implies more: advanced packaging at roughly 8–10% of a ~US$165bn 2026 revenue run-rate is US$13.2–16.5bn, of which Epoch models NVIDIA taking 63–70% across perhaps six to eight million accelerator packages, implying US$1,040–1,925 per part. The two ranges overlap below US$1,200 and the top-down mid-point of about US$1,480 is 1.3x Epoch's US$1,100. The gap that remains is that TSMC's advanced-packaging line also includes InFO, SoIC, mask and test work and is priced at a healthy margin. On either angle the packaging step is between 2.6% and 6.4% of the accelerator's selling price while its capacity determines the whole of the throughput.

The customer's return on buying ASE's service is therefore insensitive to ASE's price. A 20% increase on that layer costs the customer well under 1.5% of chip selling price.▪ The same 20% applied to guided 2026 LEAP revenue above US$3.5bn is more than US$700m of incremental revenue at close to 100% incremental margin, against 1H26 net income attributable to the parent of NT$35,200m (about US$1.1bn). That is the economic definition of a supplier with latent pricing power, and management is deliberately not using all of it: "The price hike is not part of the structure margin… in general, we do not comment on the price increase with customers" (Q4 2025 call).

The binding constraint: ABF and IC-substrate supply comes from a concentrated external base and is tight at the industry level, while ASE's own 2026 constraint is equipment and buildings. The FY2025 20-F names Kinsus, Nan Ya PCB and Unimicron and calls the market concentrated; it names ABF by material and gives a mechanism ("may face a higher risk of supply shortages or extended lead times due to potential strong demand for AI, elevated manufacturing difficulty, and heavy capital requirements for capacity expansion"); and it states ASE cannot relieve it, self-supplying 8.7% of consolidated substrate requirements by value and expecting internal operations not to meet requirements "for the foreseeable future."

FY Substrate self-supply, % of consolidated requirements by value
2016 29.7%
2018 14.2%
2020 10.1%
2022 8.5%
2023 6.6%
2024 6.8%
2025 8.7%

ASE's own hedge against the substrate layer has shrunk by roughly two-thirds while the mix it feeds became more substrate-intensive.

Management named its own constraint without hedging on the 2Q26 call, "Our capability for near-term incremental growth is being gated by our abilities to install capital equipment and build out our buildings and facilities," and in Q3 2025 said of a possible substrate shortage, "at this time, we haven't seen any real disruptions on our service to our customers… being the dominant player, if there's any problem, we're the ones that our customers come to." The last time ASE called substrate a hard gate was 2021–22. Substrate is the structural constraint; equipment lead times and building construction are the operative ones in 2026.▪

The equipment interface is where the filing language is weakest for ASE: "The market for semiconductor equipment is characterized by intense demand, limited supply, and long delivery cycles… We have no binding supply agreements with any of our vendors and acquire our equipment on a purchase order basis." ASE's FY2026 plan of about US$10.5bn is roughly 85% of FY2025 ATM revenue, and testing-equipment capex alone was US$804m in 2Q26, annualising at US$3.2bn, above Teradyne's entire FY2025 revenue of US$3,191m.

Who is locking up whom: ASE has committed US$4.3bn of unpaid capital orders and US$9.0bn of three-year contractual obligations with no binding customer volume commitment on the other side. It holds no material backlog and prices weeks before delivery. Amkor discloses the same shape. Ajinomoto notified substrate makers of a roughly 30% film price increase effective 3Q26 (finance.biggo.com and digitimes.com, both accessed 2026-08-03) [web]; finished ABF substrate lead times run 16–24 weeks, and about 28 weeks for the 14–16-layer parts used in AI accelerators [web, directional trade-press figures]. ASE's ATM raw-material ratio has been 28% for four straight quarters, so the 3Q26 and 4Q26 ATM raw-material percentage is the cleanest single test of whether the upstream squeeze reaches ASE's income statement.

Customer-side economics one layer out: the hyperscalers funding the chain are spending roughly US$700bn in calendar 2026 across Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, with about US$434bn spent in the four quarters to March 2026 [web]. Those four plus Oracle depreciate cloud server and network equipment over six years on roughly US$467bn of net PP&E entering 2026, and a credible bear case argues the economic life of GPU-based hardware is nearer two to three years, implying about US$176bn of understated depreciation across 2026–28 (footnotebrief.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. That is the single external assumption on which the durability of ASE's LEAP revenue rests. It does not affect 2026 or 2027, which are gated by ASE's own installation schedule. The leading indicator is hyperscaler capex guidance rather than hyperscaler profitability, because a depreciation-life reset compresses reported earnings before it compresses unit demand.

Circular flows: there is no vendor financing, no equity stake in a customer of any size, and no prepayment funding supplier capacity. What exists instead runs in ASE's favour: customer-consigned wafers remove its largest input from its balance sheet; customer-consigned test equipment finances part of its capex at the margin; leased testers offload residual-value risk into right-of-use assets of NT$13,996m; and asset-related government grants are recognised as deferred revenue rather than netted against cost. ASE has pledged NT$52,372m of assets against bank borrowings and tariff guarantees on imported raw materials. And ASE's factory buildings, the constraint it names on its own growth, are partly built by Hung Ching Development & Construction, a 26.22%-owned equity-method investee that also owns ASE common shares, with NT$9,494m of resolved purchases across 2024–25.

Through FY2025 the consolidated top line had still not regained its FY2022 peak. Every dollar of ATM growth over FY2022 to FY2025 came from the computing end market; communications shrank, and the automotive, consumer and industrial third of the business was flat in absolute terms.▪

The unit-driven part of ASE's business tracks wafer area, which grew 5.8%. ASE ATM grew 23.7% in US dollars. The 18-point gap is content per wafer plus price plus mix.▪ The industry-dollar comparison is misleading for 2026: WSTS forecasts a US$1.51tn market with memory alone above US$800bn, and ASE packages no memory: its service description covers logic, mixed-signal, RF and SiP/MEMS/discrete modules and never lists DRAM or NAND. ATM here is management's basis — packaging, testing, direct material and others — translated at each year's average rate, so FY2025 is US$12.56bn against the audited segment note's US$12.11bn in §4.1. The FY2026 LEAP figure is the residual of the guided +35% ATM line and the guided +20% general line, which is why it sits above the guided US$3.5bn.

The claimed secular driver did appear in the numbers, and it did not account for a majority of the growth in either year. In FY2025 LEAP contributed 41% of the ATM revenue increment and the mainstream business 59%; on the FY2026 guide the split is roughly even.▪ The framing that ASE's growth "is AI" is half-true by dollars.

The mainstream half is an industry-wide cyclical recovery rather than ASE share gain.▪ Amkor's mainstream wirebond product group grew 21.0% in 1H26 and its advanced products 27.8%, while ASE's general-segment guide moved from +13% to +20% between the Q1 and Q2 2026 calls. Splitting the peer cohort by exposure: the AI-test cohort (King Yuan, ASE Testing) grew 30%+ in 2025; the volume cohort (Amkor +6.2%, Powertech ~+2%, JCET +8.1%, wafer area +5.8%) grew 2–8%. ASE ATM at +23.7% sat between them, as its 6%/94% LEAP-versus-general mix implies.

Part of ASE's mainstream outperformance is acquired. The Infineon Philippines and South Korea sites completed on 2024-08-01, and ASE never discloses acquired revenue. Sizing from the employee table, where Philippines headcount goes 0 to 891 to 818 and Korea 2,399 to 2,780 to 3,053, gives 1,472–1,545 acquired heads at a group revenue per employee of NT$6.09m, or NT$9.0–9.4bn of annualised revenue, of which FY2025 captured seven additional months [estimate: headcount-proportional bound]. That is NT$5.2–5.5bn, US$0.17bn, against a US$2.41bn ATM increment: about 7% of the growth, so organic ATM growth in FY2025 was roughly +22% and the organic general segment +13%.

Management set the benchmark itself, twice, and has not met it.▪ "Our ATM business to outgrow the logic semiconductor market" (Q4 2024 call, for 2025) produced +23.7% against WSTS logic at +39.9%, an underperformance of about 16 points. The 2026 guide of +35% sits just below the +37% logic forecast. The mechanical defence is real: logic dollars capitalise the value of the die and its HBM, while an OSAT bills a service fee unrelated to the die's value, so a US$30k accelerator inflates the logic market far more than it inflates ASE's revenue.

6.2 Cyclical versus secular in 2026

Utilization: blended ATM utilization went "around 60%" (1Q24), "mid- to high 60s" (4Q24), "slightly above 65%" expected for 1Q25, "high 70s" (3Q25), "around 80%" (4Q25 and 1Q26), "between 80% to 85%" (2Q26). That is a cyclical recovery and it is finite. Management's own map puts about 85% at a 30% ATM gross margin, and the 2Q26 call added: "Effectively, outside of equipment lines being placed into service, capacities were generally very close to being full."

Mainstream pricing, which the 20-F says should not be happening: derived from the disclosed quarterly ATM revenue and the disclosed whole-percent wirebonding mix:
