[estimate: mix percentages are disclosed as whole integers, so each cell inherits roughly ±2% of error and the year-over-year wirebonding growth in 2Q26 spans +12% to +21%]

The fleet is 2.0% smaller than six quarters ago and produces 29.5% more revenue per unit. That combines utilization, mix and price, and the three cannot be separated from disclosure. Management confirms the price component qualitatively: asked directly whether ASE was hiking prices aggressively, the CFO answered "I think we are still in a very, very kind of a friendly pricing environment… we can definitely pass on these cost increases to our customers through our pricing arrangements." Two named input costs moved hard over the same window — ABF film up about 30% effective 3Q26 [web], and gold from roughly US$2,050/oz in 2023 to about US$4,550/oz at end-2025 [web] — so an unknown share of the revenue-per-bonder gain is cost pass-through rather than margin. The commodity end is producing record revenue per installed tool against a multi-decade base rate of price deflation.

Test has switched from price-led to capacity-led. Revenue per tester per quarter went NT$2.494m (4Q24), NT$2.394m (1Q25), NT$2.835m (4Q25), NT$2.774m (1Q26), NT$2.835m (2Q26). It rose 18% from 1Q25 through 4Q25 and then went flat while the fleet grew 13.4% in two quarters. Management's explanation is consistent: "we will continue to see gradually increasing depreciation without significant amounts of associated revenue during the tuning and qualification period."

The 3Q26 EMS acceleration is a memory pass-through. Management guided EMS revenue up around 40% sequentially, from NT$65,789m to roughly NT$92bn, and explained it on the same call: "this is largely because of the component price hikes, particularly in the memory sector. So if you take that part of the number out, I think the third quarter EMS should see a typical seasonality kind of movement," with memory confirmed as "a pass-through type of cost." That EMS step alone is roughly 14 points of the 21–22% consolidated sequential guide. Solving the guided operating income against management's ex-pass-through margin of 3.7–3.8% implies an underlying sequential increase of 18–29% and a pass-through component of NT$7,468–14,543m, which is 28–55% of the entire sequential increase [estimate: solve the guided operating income for the underlying revenue base]. TrendForce reported conventional DRAM contract prices up 90–95% sequentially in 1Q26 and 58–63% in 2Q26, with NAND up 55–60% then 70–75% (trendforce.com and trendforce.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. In a business where raw materials are 79% of revenue and prices are confirmed weeks before delivery, that flows to the revenue line almost immediately and to gross profit not at all.

6.3 Technology and policy shifts that change the slope

Shift Mechanism What shows first
Panel-level packaging (310×310, then 600 mm) 300 mm wafer utilization drops to ~57% at 5–6 reticle package sizes; a panel raises it to ~87% ASE's fully automated line is now guided to start production by 1Q27; slippage past that is the signal
Glass core substrate replaces organic ABF at the substrate layer "we do not have the glass substrate in production, not for the next 12 months" (Q2 2026)
Intel EMIB and embedded bridge alternative to CoWoS-class interposers ASE says it is collaborating on EMIB; a share shift appears in LEAP mix commentary before revenue
Hybrid bonding moving interconnect into the fab pulls the highest-value step into a fab-grade environment HBM4 adopting hybrid bonding; ASE discloses no hybrid-bonding programme while Amkor names one
Co-packaged optics moves interconnect from copper to photons, adding packaging content test vehicles built, no production revenue disclosed after 20 years of work
Foundry in-housing TSMC CoWoS-S/L, CoPoS, SoIC; Intel EMIB and Foveros; Samsung I-Cube ASE's on-substrate share of LEAP declining, or the outsourced wafer allocation falling

Geography and policy: the 6-K safe-harbour list now names "the recent shift in United States trade policies." Management's answer is "Taiwan Plus One", with Penang as the main non-Taiwan build plus Korea and the Philippines, and an explicit doctrine that wafers produced in Taiwan get packaged in Taiwan while the non-Taiwan footprint exists to catch wafers produced elsewhere. Leading-edge work stays home until the process is mastered: "before we have a full confidence we can fully execute the ramp with reasonable results, we will not go outside of Taiwan" (Q4 2024 call). Taiwan generated 58.9% of FY2025 operating revenues, up from 55.1% and the highest since FY2022, in the year the diversification story was loudest.

Revenue is also shifting toward Taiwan-headquartered counterparties: US-headquartered customers were 63.6% of operating revenues in FY2023, 60.2% in FY2024 and 56.7% in FY2025, while Taiwan rose from 12.1% to 18.0%. The 20-F states only that "We categorize our operating revenues geographically based on the country in which the customer is headquartered," and the table covers all revenue including EMS, so the shift is a disclosed fact without a disclosed cause.

Quarterly tells: wirebonding revenue per wire bonder, which is the mainstream price regime; testing revenue per tester, already flat while the fleet grows 13%; computing as a share of ATM revenue, 30% in 2Q26 against 15.8% in FY2022; the LEAP dollar guide itself, revised up three times in nine months, where the first flat or trimmed revision arrives on a call before it arrives in a filing; IDM share of ATM revenue; the >10% customer's annual NT$ disclosure; equipment capex against ATM EBITDA, where 2Q26 equipment capex of US$1,695m already exceeds segment EBITDA; and the wire bonder count, falling for six straight quarters.

7. Critical points

1. The capex is being installed ahead of the revenue, funded with debt, into a cost base that cannot be unwound. Cash capex was NT$164,643m in FY2025 against operating cash flow of NT$142,249m, the first year in the decade in which capex exceeded operating cash flow. In 1H26 the ratio went to 149%: operating cash flow NT$83,401m against PP&E payments of NT$123,941m, so free cash flow of −NT$40,540m in six months already exceeds the whole of FY2025's −NT$22,394m. Total interest-bearing debt rose from NT$213,868m (2024-12-31) to NT$306,200m (2026-06-30), +43.2% in eighteen months, with NT$40,900m of that added in 2Q26 alone. FY2026 capex is guided at about US$10.5bn, US$4.0bn of buildings and facilities plus US$6.5bn of equipment, of which 70% is leading-edge, across 13 greenfield and 8 brownfield construction projects. Against that, NT$114,686m of contracted equipment purchases sits unpaid at 2025-12-31 and no backlog, take-or-pay or minimum-volume commitment is disclosed anywhere on the customer side. The CFO's own framing: "the negative cash flow situation will remain for some time."

2. The depreciation from that capex lands whether or not the demand does, and the last downcycle shows what that costs. In FY2023 a 13.3% revenue decline produced a 48.7% operating-profit decline, a realized decremental operating margin of 44.4%. D&A is already running at NT$20,000m per quarter (NT$80,000m annualised) against NT$67,440m for all of FY2025, and packaging depreciation should roughly double over three to four years on FY2025 capex of NT$113,392m against FY2025 packaging D&A and rental of NT$37,261m. The FY2025 20-F added a risk factor that names the mechanism in its own words: a significant reduction in AI-related demand "would lead to lower utilization rates for our specialized equipment and facilities, potentially resulting in stranded assets, margin compression and a material adverse effect." Applying the FY2023 decremental to the 2Q26 annualised revenue base of roughly NT$764,000m, a repeat 13.3% decline removes about NT$45,000m of operating profit against a 2Q26 annualised operating profit near NT$84,600m, before any of the incremental depreciation from FY2026–27 capex enters the cost base.

3. One unnamed customer is 25.0% of revenue, and the risk factor that used to quantify that was cut. NT$161,282,046 thousand of FY2025 operating revenues came from one customer spanning packaging and EMS, including OEMs manufacturing on its behalf. It is named nowhere in any filing or transcript in the archive, and its revenue declined 7.6% in FY2025 while packaging grew 17.8%. Losing a quarter of it removes roughly NT$40,300m of revenue and, at the FY2023 decremental, about NT$17,900m of operating profit, or 35% of FY2025's total. Every 20-F from FY2016 through FY2024 quantified customer concentration inside the risk factor; the FY2025 filing removed both sentences. The figures survive in Item 4.B and Note 41(c), but the risk factors no longer carry the number. Amkor, by contrast, names Apple at 29.8% of FY2025 net sales and Qualcomm at 11.1%.

4. A third party allocates the volume in ASE's fastest-growing business. LEAP went from 6% of ATM revenue in FY2024 to 13% in FY2025 and is guided above US$3.5bn for FY2026, roughly a fifth of ATM revenue, with a doubling targeted for 2027. Roughly two-thirds of it is on-substrate work allocated out of a foundry partner's flow, about 19% is wafer probe, and under 10% is ASE's own architecture end to end. Asked what happens to ASE's role as the lead foundry partner moves toward 3D and panel-level packaging, the COO answered: "there are packaging that needs to be taken by the foundry people because access to the leading edge wafer is simply not available to the others… That is a domain that the pure-play wafer people needs to decide… In terms of future, we do not know." ATM was 66% of 2Q26 revenue and 94% of operating profit, up from 61% and 87% a year earlier, so an adverse re-allocation lands on the highest-margin, highest-capex part of the business.▪

5. Utilization is the disclosed margin driver and it is never disclosed, and the headroom is nearly used. The FY2025 20-F names capacity utilization as the determinant of gross margin in fourteen places and gives a number in none. Management gives one on every call: roughly 65% expected for 1Q25, high-70s in 3Q25, around 80% in 4Q25 and 1Q26, 80–85% in 2Q26. Its published map puts 70% at a 24% ATM gross margin and about 85% at 30%, and 4Q26 ATM gross margin is guided above 30%. From here, further margin has to come from price or mix rather than from filling factories, and price is the question management declines to answer: "I can never give you a direct answer on whether we're going to raise our prices or not."

6. FY2025 was the segment's worst conversion of growth into profit in a decade, and 1H26 reversed it. Packaging revenue grew 17.8% in FY2025 and segment pre-tax profit rose NT$2,090m, an incremental pre-tax margin of 4.5% against a six-year average of 21.4% and 32–50% in prior up-cycles. Testing's best revenue year produced its second-lowest incremental pre-tax margin of the last seven, 25.8% against 42.6% in 2022 and 65.9% in 2021. Management explained it in advance: LEAP lines must be installed as a full set and absorb depreciation through tuning and qualification. The first half of 2026 is the reversal: ATM incremental gross margin of 40.2% and incremental operating margin of 31.2%. The FY2025 experience is the base rate for the first year of each capacity wave, and management has guided to a doubling of LEAP in 2027 on FY2026 capex of US$10.5bn.

7. The margin premium over Amkor is real and does not reach the capital line. ASE's ATM pre-tax margin premium over Amkor has run 3.5 to 6.4 points since FY2019 and was 5.5 points in FY2025, on a gross-margin premium of 9.5 points. Estimated packaging ROIC was 8.6% in FY2025 against Amkor's 9.5% computed the same way, and was 7.8 and 6.2 points below Amkor at the FY2021–22 peak. The reconciliation is capital intensity: 36.8% of packaging revenue against Amkor's 13.5%. Over a full cycle FY2019 to FY2025, group ROIIC was +14.0%, respectable and not exceptional.

8. Roughly 40% of revenue is EMS, and it contributes almost nothing. EMS was 39.9% of FY2025 revenue, 14.9% of segment pre-tax profit, 7.0% of group goodwill and 3.4% of segment capital expenditure. In 2Q26 it was 34% of revenue and 6% of operating profit. It has the lowest operating margin of the five-company contract-manufacturing peer set, on a gross margin at the middle of the pack, and the whole gap is an operating-expense ratio 130–250bp above every peer. The 3Q26 guide of +40% sequential revenue is, by management's own account, largely memory component-price pass-through at close to zero incremental margin.

9. The balance sheet is being rebuilt into a shape it has not had before while the leverage ratio falls. Net debt to EBITDA went from 1.52x at end-2025 to roughly 1.28x on a trailing basis at 2Q26, so the ratio says deleveraging. Underneath, absolute debt rose 43.2% in eighteen months, floating-rate financial liabilities rose 51.6% in a single year to NT$229,258m, 86.9% of interest-bearing debt, PP&E pledged as collateral went from NT$0.9m to NT$34,209m, and 63.4% of long-term debt matures in calendar 2027. The disclosed 100bp interest-rate sensitivity nearly tripled in two years, from NT$660m to NT$1,833m, which is 3.6% of FY2025 pre-tax profit and scales to roughly NT$2.2bn at 2Q26 debt levels [estimate: NT$1,833m × NT$306,200m ÷ the NT$253bn of gross debt at 2025-12-31].

10. NT$30.5bn of funding arrived in FY2025 through an unexplained liability line. Other non-current liabilities went NT$5,825m (2023) to NT$7,057m (2024) to NT$37,585m (2025), and on the 6-K basis kept climbing to NT$90,750m by 2Q26. There is no line-item breakdown in the 20-F. The only candidates the filing identifies are customer advance payments under long-term agreements and asset-related government grants recognised as deferred revenue. If it is the former, customers are pre-funding a material share of the LEAP build interest-free and the debt-funded framing is incomplete; if it is the latter, it is a subsidy releasing into other income over the assets' lives. Management has never mentioned it on any call in the archive.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"AI advanced packaging is transforming ASE's packaging economics." Packaging revenue in FY2025 exceeded the FY2022 peak by 1.4%, and packaging gross margin was 22.1% against 27.1%, with segment pre-tax margin 10.1% against 17.1%. Segment pre-tax profit of NT$31,039m was 40.1% below the FY2022 figure on higher revenue. The advanced share of packaging revenue rose from 41.2% (2021) to 59.6% (2025), 18.4 points, while segment gross margin declined 3.6 points.▪ The accretive-mix claim is true at the gross-profit line on incremental leading-edge business and was false at the segment line for three years, because the depreciation of the capacity built to serve it arrived before the utilization did. The 1H26 ATM data — 26.7% gross margin, 40.2% incremental — is the first evidence the claim will hold, and it is two quarters old.

"ASE is a CoWoS outsourcing play." TSMC is reported to be outsourcing 240,000–270,000 CoWoS wafers in 2026, of which SPIL takes 60,000–80,000 and Amkor 180,000–190,000 (eu.36kr.com and digitimes.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. No reliable per-wafer price is publicly documented, so the dollar bound cannot be closed from that direction. ASE's own disclosure does bound it: full-process work is guided at about 10% of LEAP revenue in 2026, up from about 3% in 2025. The great majority of LEAP packaging revenue is therefore not TSMC-farmed CoWoS but ASE's own advanced flip-chip and fan-out work — FOCoS, FOCoS-Bridge, high-layer-count FCBGA for AI ASICs and networking switches, and wafer bumping — sold directly. The distinction matters because the two have different exposure to a single foundry's allocation decisions.

"Wirebonding is the legacy drag that AI is replacing." Wirebonding was 32.9% of packaging revenue in FY2025, NT$101,445m, roughly 2.7x the estimated LEAP packaging revenue of NT$37,800m. Revenue per installed tool rose 29.5% between 4Q24 and 2Q26 on a fleet that shrank 2.0%. It is not shrinking in dollars; it is roughly flat near NT$100bn while everything else grows around it, and it contributed 14% of FY2025 packaging growth. The correct characterisation is a large, cash-generative, fully depreciated annuity on trailing-edge unit volume, with revenue per tool still 21% below its FY2021 peak.▪

"High fixed costs mean high operating leverage." They mean high leverage in both directions and the coefficients are asymmetric. In testing, the decremental pre-tax margin in the FY2023 downturn was 85.4% and the incremental in the FY2025 upturn 25.8%, more than three times worse on the way down. At group level the FY2023 decremental operating margin was 44.4% against a best-ever single-year incremental of 30.0%. Fixed costs cut hardest in the year depreciation is installed ahead of revenue.

"The largest customer is the AI relationship." The single >10% customer spans packaging and EMS, and its revenue declined 7.6% in FY2025 (NT$174,486m to NT$161,282m) in the year packaging grew 17.8%. That profile fits a consumer-module relationship rather than an AI accelerator one. The AI revenue is arriving through a different customer set, and on the ATM top-five trend of 41% to 44% in three quarters, a more concentrated one.

"ASE is an AI advanced-packaging leader." Its own architecture is under 10% of LEAP revenue and under 2% of ATM revenue in 2026. Two-thirds of LEAP is discrete steps allocated out of a foundry partner's flow and roughly a quarter is test. ASE is the largest and best-capitalised executor of the AI packaging build-out; the architecture-level leadership is TSMC's.▪

"Margins are rising because the mix is shifting to differentiated technology." ASE's own structural framework maps 70% utilization to a 24% ATM gross margin and about 85% to 30%. Blended utilization was 80–85% in 2Q26 and ATM gross margin was 27.3%, which is close to where the utilization curve predicts before any mix effect. Asked what drives the move through the ceiling, the CFO listed "margin accretive business growth… improvement in efficiency… continuous expansion of our automated factories. Operating leverage does — of course, it plays a very important role." Asked about price, he described a friendly environment and cost pass-through rather than a technology premium.

"R&D spending proves the technology lead." R&D rose 14.0% in FY2025 to 5.1% of revenue, twice Amkor's 2.5%. Over the same period the granted patent estate declined 1.2% and pending applications 4.3%, and the redistribution-layer and wafer-level foundations remain licensed non-exclusively from Infineon, TDK and DECA. The spending is buying process ramp and qualification capacity, which is what a fast follower buys.

"Foundry competition is a new FY2025 risk." The sentence "some foundry players have actively invested and expanded their advanced packaging capacity and gained some customer bases with their services and solutions" appears in the FY2021, FY2022, FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 risk factors and in none of FY2016 through FY2020, with the FY2021 wording differing slightly. Foundry competition entered the risk factors with the FY2021 filing, four years earlier than commonly stated. What actually changed in FY2025 is the removal of quantification: customer concentration, FX loss history, impairment history and the share-option overhang were all deleted from the risk factors with no replacement figures, and the named competitor JCET and named suppliers LG Innotek, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Toppan were dropped across FY2023 to FY2025. The FY2025 risk section is longer (99,288 characters against 98,682) and less specific.

"ASE has 45% of the OSAT market." The figure values ASE at holding-company revenue, including a contract-electronics business that does no semiconductor packaging, while every other player in the same table is measured on OSAT revenue only. Corrected to an assembly-and-test basis, ASE's share of the top-ten is 30.3% (2024) and 32.2% (2025), and its share of the whole outsourced market including the tail is 24–27%.

"Chinese OSATs are taking share from ASE." JCET, Tongfu and Tianshui Huatian went from 31.2% of top-ten revenue in 2024 to 31.2% in 2025, growing 13.7% against a market that grew 13.6%. China's three largest OSATs added US$1.42bn of revenue in 2025; ASE added US$2.08bn on its assembly-and-test business alone. The share that moved came from Amkor.

"The structural gross-margin range is a forecast." It was left unrevised through two full years of being missed to the downside — FY2023 at 21.8% and FY2024 at 22.5% against a 24% floor that had itself been cut from "mid-20s" in the same quarter management first warned the target was at risk — and it is now about to be breached to the upside with management saying twice that it will "review" rather than raise it. FY2025's reported 23.5% missed the range and was presented as met, on an FX-adjusted basis in one sentence and a PPA-adjusted basis in the next; those add-backs do not appear in the quarters where the target is exceeded, where 1Q26's 26.0% and 2Q26's 27.3% are quoted as reported. The range has functioned as a floor claim in the downturn and a ceiling explanation in the upturn.▪

"ASE guides conservatively." The claim is too weak for the ATM lines and too strong for EMS. Across 108 guided line items over 24 quarters, ATM revenue beat 71% of the time with one miss in six years and ATM gross margin beat 79%; in the numeric-range era the ATM gross margin came in 30 to 370bp above the top of the guided band in four consecutive quarters, a mean of +149bp excluding the one FX miss. EMS revenue beat 46% and EMS operating margin 38%, and EMS accounts for six of the eight total misses. A model built on the guidance midpoint is structurally low on ATM and roughly right on EMS. Part of the beat streak is currency: the assumed rate moved from 29.2 for 3Q25 to 31.9 for 3Q26, and on management's own rule of thumb of 0.4pp of holding-company gross margin per 1% of NT dollar move, that 9% is worth roughly 3.5 points of gross margin [estimate: 9% × 0.4pp, applying the rule stated on the 4Q20 call]. Management gave a precise FX bridge when currency hurt and has not given one on the way up.

"The 2027 doubling is a demand statement." Management frames it as an installation problem: "whatever that target has been achieved by year-end, with the next 12 months, building new facility and adding new machines, we will be able to double that." No backlog, take-or-pay or minimum-volume commitment is disclosed anywhere, against NT$114,686m of unpaid equipment obligations. LEAP is also undefined in any filing, and its FY2026 target moved from US$2.6bn to US$3.2bn to US$3.5bn to "ahead of 3.5" in nine months, three upward revisions off a FY2025 base of US$1.6bn; without a definition, the split between demand and reclassification is not observable.▪

"ASE is not converting its bargaining position into price." Management excludes price increases from the structural-margin framework, calls them "opportunistic," and declines to discuss them with investors. In the same period it describes a "favorable" and "friendly" pricing environment and confirms cost pass-through, and trade coverage reports advanced-packaging quotes up more than 20% in mid-2026 [web, unverified]. Price is contributing; management neither quantifies it nor builds it into the framework it gives investors.

"The AI mix shift de-risks the business." LEAP is roughly a fifth of ATM revenue in FY2026 and management aims to double it in 2027, while ATM already generates 94% of group operating profit on 66% of revenue, up from 87% on 61% a year earlier. Testing capex is 71.8% of testing segment revenue and packaging capex 36.8%, against EMS at 2.3%; group capex to operating cash flow moved from 47% (FY2023) to 149% (1H26). A diversified, low-capital-intensity revenue base is being converted into a concentrated, high-fixed-cost one whose allocation is decided by a third party, and the last cycle's realized decremental was 44.4%.

"The 2Q26 print was a large company-specific beat." The ADR rose 11.7% on 2026-07-30, but the SOX rose 8.2% and Amkor rose 12.9% the same session, leaving +3.5 points of company-specific move. The largest company-specific reaction in the twelve-quarter record was the 4Q25 print on 2026-02-05: +6.8 points against the SOX and +25.0% over five sessions, when 2026 LEAP revenue was guided to double to US$3.2bn. Separately, 2Q26 pre-tax income included NT$4,566m of net non-operating gains, inside which management described NT$5.7bn of items as "potentially nonrecurring" — mark-to-market equity gains of NT$4.2bn and FX hedging gains of NT$1.5bn — against NT$1.1bn of other non-operating costs. Removing those at the quarter's 16.4% effective rate takes EPS from NT$4.80 to about NT$3.72 against a NT$3.80 consensus [estimate: flagged nonrecurring items removed at the disclosed effective rate].

2024-02 First public leading-edge target: revenue to double in 2024 LEAP becomes a disclosed line, on calls only
2024-08-01 Acquires Infineon's Philippines and South Korea back-end sites for NT$3,042m combined Bargain-purchase gain on one, zero goodwill on the other, supply agreements attached
2025-Q2 NT dollar appreciates 4.9% within the quarter; net income attributable declines to NT$7,521m The only material guidance miss in six years, and it was currency
2026-02-05 FY2025 results: LEAP US$1.6bn and 13% of ATM; 2026 LEAP guided to double to US$3.2bn The largest company-specific share-price reaction of the twelve-quarter record
2026-03 ASE Malaysia's board resolves to acquire Analog Devices' Malaysian subsidiaries for US$108.8m The captive-site playbook continues
2026-03-27 Board resolves a NT$6.6 per share dividend, roughly NT$29,438m, a record Paid into the largest negative free-cash-flow year in company history
2026-07-30 2Q26: record ATM revenue NT$126,148m, ATM gross margin 27.3%, utilization 80–85%; FY2026 capex raised again to ~US$10.5bn Capex now exceeds EBITDA on a quarterly basis

Five inflections, in date order:

  • The SPIL acquisition (2015–2020). Total consideration NT$168,440,585 thousand, goodwill NT$39,990,231 thousand, identifiable intangibles NT$31,354,386 thousand, net cash out at close NT$95,241,855 thousand. For the first two years the deal made the company worse: revenue rose from NT$290,441m (FY2017, ASE alone) to NT$413,182m (FY2019) while operating margin declined from 8.7% to 5.6% and profit attributable declined from NT$22,819m to NT$17,061m, with NT$4,797m of purchase-price-allocation charges running through FY2019 gross profit. The reason is in the timeline: the regulator required independent operation for 24 months and all conditions were lifted only on 2020-03-25. Once they were, and once the cycle turned, packaging gross margin moved from 17.4% (2019) to 27.1% (2022) on a business whose margin had been pinned at 22.8% in both 2016 and 2017. ASE initiated the deal, and its price included a legal overhang that is still open: the insider-trading prosecution of the COO arising from the tender offers has produced a not-guilty judgment (2020), a Supreme Court reversal, a 22-month guilty sentence (2024-12-31), another Supreme Court reversal (2025-07-10), a second not-guilty affirmation (2026-02-11) and a further prosecution appeal (2026-03-02).
  • September 2020, losing a fifth of ATM revenue overnight. Export controls removed a customer at roughly 20% of ATM revenue and cost NT$1.6bn of charges in the quarter. Within the same quarter loading "snapped back to full utilization," and by the Q3 2020 Q&A 75% of the vacated capacity was backfilled with the remainder guided to 1Q21. FY2020 ATM revenue still grew 12%. The largest concentration shock in the record cost one quarter of margin and nothing structural, which is a fact about the business model: ASE sells machine time and floor space, and when a customer disappears the capacity is re-tooled. The industry was in shortage at the time.
  • December 2021, exiting China at a gain and concentrating on Taiwan. Six sites sold at 1.89x carrying value, 7.6% of 2021 ATM revenue and 4,221 wire bonders plus 1,522 testers out of the fleet, and the remaining footprint more than replaced the volume within twelve months. The part management no longer revisits: 28.5% of the price, NT$10,533,600 thousand, was never paid in cash. Its due date was extended from six to fifteen months and it was then settled in a 16.48% unlisted minority stake in Hongkong United Ascend Holdings Limited, completed in September 2024, recorded at Level 3 fair value equal to its US$380m cost and never marked.
  • 2023, the fixed-cost base exposed and the structural-margin claim broken. Management guided FY2023 ATM revenue "flattish to high single-digit decline" with a 1Q trough and sequential recovery, and reiterated a "mid-20%s to 30%" ATM structural gross margin. Actual ATM revenue declined 15%, ATM gross margin came in at 21.8%, and 4Q23 ATM revenue was below 3Q23's. Group operating profit halved on a 13.3% revenue decline. By the Q3 2024 call the structural floor had become 24%, and the FY2024 result of 22.5% was described as "a bit short of our structural gross margin target of 24%", and that target had been 25% eighteen months earlier.
  • 2024–2026, the LEAP and test capex regime change. LEAP revenue went US$250m, US$600m, US$1.6bn, guided above US$3.5bn. Machinery capex went US$0.914bn (2023), US$1.876bn (2024), US$3.4bn (2025), US$6.5bn planned (2026), with US$4.0bn of buildings on top. Testers went from 4,918 (FY2021) to 8,348 (2Q26), +70%, while wire bonders went from 26,555 (FY2020) to 24,815, −6.6%. ASE has stopped growing the asset that defined it for thirty years. Total interest-bearing debt went NT$191.7bn (4Q23) to NT$306.2bn (2Q26), and net debt to equity from 0.38 to 0.47 on that debt definition, against 32% (FY2023) to 43% (FY2025) on the lease-excluded gross-debt basis of the §10.4 table. Unlike 2015–2018, this is not an acquisition: since SPIL, ASE has spent NT$12bn of cash on acquisitions, 7% of what SPIL alone cost.

How the company behaves: in a downturn it cuts equipment capex hard and protects the growth asset: 2023 machinery capex was halved while test investment was explicitly ring-fenced and building spend continued. It does not appear to cut price; the 2023 language was "pricing resiliency." In an upturn it re-levers quickly and without a stated ceiling: capex went from NT$48.8bn (2023, accrual basis) to a planned NT$330bn (2026), roughly sevenfold in three years, and the stated framework is "we will remain aggressive in CapEx spending… to further extend our lead over competition." It buys captive back-end plants from its own customers cheaply and turns the seller into a customer. It exits at a gain rather than writing down: the China disposal produced a NT$17,340m net gain and no SPIL goodwill impairment has ever been taken. And when it misses a target it restates the target rather than the strategy: the structural ATM gross-margin range moved from "mid-20s to 30%" to "24% to 30%" in 2H24, and the FY2023 revenue guidance was never formally retracted.

Episodes the current account omits: the testing gross margin stopped being disclosed as testing became the story: through FY2023 the 20-F gave packaging, testing and EMS gross margins separately and testing's ran 30.7%–37.6%; from FY2024 packaging and testing are one line. Testing revenue then grew 31.8% in 2025 and took 40% of the 2026 equipment capex budget on about 19% of ATM revenue. The phrase "leading-edge advanced packaging" appears zero times in every call from 2Q20 through 3Q23 and first appears in the Q4 2023 call; before that "advanced packaging" meant the far broader bumping/flip-chip/WLP/SiP bundle, so the "2022 advanced packaging revenue grew 27%" statement is not comparable to the US$250m LEAP figure for 2023 disclosed a year later.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs the company

ASEH has no chief executive officer. Jason Chang was styled "chairman and chief executive officer" through the FY2020 20-F; from FY2021 onward every 20-F calls him "chairman and principal executive officer," the SEC certification term, and the CEO title sits at the operating subsidiary with Tien Wu as CEO of ASE Inc. No filing explains the change.

Officer Role Age Years with the group
Jason C.S. Chang Chairman 81 42
Richard H.P. Chang Vice Chairman and President 79 42
Tien Wu Chief Operating Officer 68 26
Joseph Tung Chief Financial Officer 67 31
Du-Tsuen Uang Chief Administration, Governance and Risk Officer 66 23

All five have been in place since ASEH's founding in April 2018, and no successor is named for any of them in any filing. Turnover in the FY2024 to FY2025 executive rosters is confined to divisional general managers, and every change traces to a death, a retirement or an acquisition.

The board has nine seats and three independent directors. Five of the nine represent ASE Enterprises Limited, a Hong Kong company holding 15.37% of ASEH whose shares sit under a revocable Bahamas trust for the benefit of the chairman and his family; the trust redomiciled from Guernsey to the Bahamas on 2025-02-04 with no reason given. Under R.O.C. law, "Persons designated to represent corporate or government shareholders as directors are nominated by such shareholders at the shareholders' meeting and may be replaced as representatives by such shareholders at will." Four of the nine seats are family: the chairman, his brother, his son-in-law Andrew Tang (added 2024) and his daughter Dan-Yao Chang (added June 2025, four months after the death of the chairman's son Rutherford Chang, whose seat she took). The chairman attended 12 of 14 board meetings in 2024, the lowest attendance of any continuing director; all three independent directors attended 100%.

10.2 What they are paid, and against what

The 20-F discloses one aggregate number for all directors and executive officers.

The plan flexed down once in seven years, in FY2023, when it flexed almost fully (−41.3% pay on −47.9% profit). In the two other down years it rose: FY2019 +10.4% on −27.1%, and FY2024 +11.9% on −2.1%. From FY2021 to FY2025 pre-tax profit declined 36.0% while remuneration rose 12.6%; FY2025 pay is 89.2% of the FY2022 peak on 62.7% of peak pre-tax profit.

Neither the 20-F nor the R.O.C. annual report names a single performance metric, weight, threshold or payout curve. The R.O.C. report says only that "In determining remuneration, both individual performance for the year and the Company's financial and financially related operational performance are considered," and that long-term incentives are restricted stock units whose "operational, performance, and ESG indicators are all closely tied to the effectiveness of future risk management." No indicator is named. The only mechanical link is the Articles' profit-share formula, whose base is absolute pre-tax profit, a size measure that rises with acquisitions and capacity additions regardless of the return on the capital deployed. Actual FY2025 draws were NT$97.3m to directors, 25% of the 0.75% cap, and NT$101.3m to employees, 20% of the 1.00% cap; together they are 9.2% of total D&O remuneration, so the formula governs less than a tenth of the pay.

Individual amounts appear only in the R.O.C. annual report, in bands. For FY2024, the chairman appears in the NT$100m-and-above band as a managerial officer and in the NT$50–100m band as a director, so his total exceeded NT$150m; each independent director received NT$2.0–3.5m, a ratio of more than 44x [web, R.O.C. Annual Report FY2024]. Restricted-stock expense of NT$52.3m for directors and NT$127.1m for the general manager and vice presidents is excluded from those bands. The benchmark group, recommended by Willis Towers Watson, is TSMC, WPG Holdings, ASUS, MediaTek, Unimicron, Powertech, King Yuan, Intel and Micron, selected "regardless of whether they belong to the semiconductor packaging and testing industry." Amkor, the only true global OSAT peer and the one ASE's own 20-F names in its M&A discussion, is absent.

The compensation committee has three members: two independent directors and Hsiao-Ying Gu, listed under the title "Other," whose disclosed qualifications are ASE Inc. project consultant of core human resource development and management, ASE Inc. HR Director, and Orient Semiconductor Electronics senior HR officer. The FY2025 20-F states separately: "We do not assess the independence of our compensation committee member(s) under the independence requirements of the NYSE listing standards but adopt the independence standard as promulgated under the R.O.C. Regulations Governing the Appointment and Exercise of Powers by the Remuneration Committee."

Equity: ASEH granted 150,000 thousand options in August 2023 at NT$107.0, a single tranche equal to about 3.4% of shares outstanding against an opening pool of 81,262 thousand, worth roughly NT$4,455m at the NT$29.7 grant-date fair value. The options are time-vesting from the second anniversary with no performance condition, and the exercise price adjusts downward for cash-dividend distributions under a formula that is not published: both plans' strikes moved −3.7% between the 2024 and 2025 balance-sheet dates. The 31 named directors and executive officers hold 12,590,000 exercisable options, 8.3% of the 151,142 thousand pool. Restricted stock does have a performance condition, and it has been enforced: the final 4,965 thousand-share tranche of the 2021 plan was forfeited in full in 2024, the year ATM gross margin came in at 22.5% against a 24% floor. The targets themselves are never published. Group share-based payment expense tripled from NT$743m (2023) to NT$2,482m (2025).

Insider ownership is one person. The chairman beneficially owns 951,100,353 shares, 21.35%, unchanged for four years with no buying and no selling. The 31 named directors and executive officers hold 25.0% of shares outstanding in total, so 85% of all insider ownership is his and the other thirty hold 3.65% combined. Fifteen of the thirty-one hold zero shares, including every overseas operating head. No insider share pledging and no related-party stock transfer is disclosed. There is no transaction-level insider record: foreign private issuers file no Forms 3, 4 or 5.

Related-party flows are concentrated in one counterparty. ASE holds 26.22% of Hung Ching Development & Construction, which holds 44,130,751 ASEH shares (0.99%), and ASE's chief administration officer sits on Hung Ching's board. Across 2024–25 ASE's board resolved NT$9,494m of property purchases from Hung Ching — NT$5,263m for a completed plant in 2024 and NT$4,231m for a 72.15% building interest in November 2025 — each at prices set by independent appraisal. The "Others" segment that houses ASE's real-estate development alongside in-house substrate production recorded a pre-tax loss of NT$2,516m in FY2025 and NT$480m of the group's NT$606m of impairment.

10.3 Candor across twenty-four calls

ASE holds no investor day; the quarterly call is the entire investor-communication surface. The commitments below show what this management treats as binding.

The target tied to a countable revenue line has been honoured; the three tied to margins and payout were redefined or dropped. Management also narrowed the LEAP definition against itself rather than widening it: "The ASE versions of leading-edge is a very leading-edge defined by our foundry customers… 7-nanometer is also advanced, but we do not count that as the leading edge."

On hostile questions the record is direct. Asked on the 2Q26 call whether quarterly capex exceeding EBITDA meant free cash flow was turning negative, the CFO answered "Yes… the negative cash flow situation will remain for some time. But at the same time, we are still maintaining a very healthy balance sheet… we are not going to be shy in making the necessary investment." Questions that would require re-anchoring a public framework get deferred rather than refused: on raising the structural range, "we will rather wait until things are more settled. Maybe next year." Management has conceded one error in six years, the FY2024 margin shortfall, and gives it an entirely external cause.

NT$ billions. Gross debt excludes lease liabilities, so it is below the company's own "total interest-bearing debt" metric.

Cumulative free cash flow over the decade was NT$185bn and cumulative dividends were NT$185bn. Every dollar of free cash went to the dividend, and everything else — NT$107bn of M&A, NT$21bn of associate stakes, NT$44bn to minorities, NT$12bn of other capital investment — was funded by debt, disposals, one equity issue of NT$10.3bn in 2017, and NT$16bn of employee option proceeds. Buybacks were NT$6bn, 0.7% of operating cash flow.

Capex, maintenance against growth: capex to D&A ran 0.85x to 1.33x from FY2016 through FY2024 and reached 2.44x in FY2025, implying roughly 59% growth spend on that proxy. On the guided FY2026 figure of about NT$330bn against D&A running near NT$80bn the ratio is about 4.1x. The proxy puts maintenance too high for a company re-mixing its asset base: over the six quarters to 2Q26 wire bonders declined 2.0% while testers rose 32.5% and quarterly ATM equipment capex rose 167%.

Returns on invested capital, and management's own yardstick: ROIC ran 8.5% (2017), 4.9% (2019), 15.0% (2022), 8.2% (2025). ROIIC was +14.0% over FY2019–FY2025, +8.3% over FY2020–FY2025, +7.1% over the full decade and −25.1% from the FY2022 peak. Asked directly for a hurdle rate on the Q2 2021 call, the CFO said "the ROE that we are looking at as the threshold is good by about 20% to 25%," and confirmed "25% for new investment." Realised ROE was 25.6% (2021) and 22.4% (2022), then 12.0%, 10.5% and 12.1%. In the four years since the threshold was named, ROE has averaged 14.3%. Asked again on the Q4 2024 call for a payback or return figure the CFO said "it's a little bit premature to pinpoint exactly what kind of return or what kind of capital intensity that's required… we would like to reserve that until later," and asked on the Q4 2025 call for a capital-intensity target the COO answered "There is no guideline."

Management's conversion rule of thumb, given on the Q3 2025 call, is that one dollar of investment creates one dollar of annual revenue, scoped explicitly to "the main businesses that we are entering now, which is OS and test," on limited data and with capacity not in full ramp. Applied to the 2026 machinery plan of about US$6.5bn it implies roughly US$6.5bn of additional annual ATM revenue capacity against an FY2025 ATM base of US$12.1bn. The record over the last three years does not support the rule at that rate: cumulative FY2023–FY2025 capex of NT$298bn accompanied a revenue decline of NT$25bn from the 2022 peak, and cumulative FY2024–FY2025 packaging capex of NT$171,958m produced a revenue increment of NT$51,537m.

Buybacks: seven programmes since 2010, each executed in full within days to weeks and then stopped. The two in the ASEH-comparable window: the March 2015 programme bought 120.0m shares at NT$44.45, an ASEH-equivalent NT$88.90 and the 82nd percentile of that year's trading range, after which the stock declined 36% to NT$57.1 by May 2016 with no further buying; and the November–December 2021 programme bought 55.0m shares at an average NT$104.27, after which the stock declined 31% to NT$72.4 by October 2022, again with no further buying. The stated purpose in the treasury-share note is "In order to maintain the Company's credit and shareholders' rights and interests." Total repurchase spend across FY2015–FY2025 was NT$11.1bn against NT$890bn of operating cash flow, about 1.2%, and Item 16E confirms zero repurchases in 2025.

Dividends: declared for the fiscal year and restated to the ASEH share basis: NT$2.80 (2016), NT$2.00 (2019), NT$7.00 (2021), NT$8.80 (2022), NT$5.20 (2023), NT$5.30 (2024), NT$6.60 (2025). Payout crossed above the stated 60–65% band on each of the last three declarations, at 70.4%, 70.5% and 70.4%. The FY2025 dividend of roughly NT$29,438m resolved on 2026-03-27 is the largest in company history, +28% on the NT$23.0bn paid in 2025, and it was declared into the largest negative free-cash-flow year on record. Cumulative dividends per share over the decade were NT$46.90 against cumulative free cash flow per share of NT$44.13. Under the Articles, cash dividends may be approved by the board alone and are reported to shareholders rather than approved by them.

Per-share value creation: on the cleaner FY2018–FY2025 window, both ends on the ASEH basis, revenue per share compounded at 7.9%, operating income per share at 9.3% and EPS at 5.9%. The gap between operating income per share and EPS is finance cost, which rose from NT$3.6bn (2018) to NT$7.5bn (2025), plus a rising minority share. Share count discipline has been good: shares issued went from 4,321.7m (2018) to 4,448.0m (2025), +2.9% over seven years net of the 55.0m cancelled in February 2022. The forward item is the option pool: 151.1m options at an average strike of NT$87.8 plus 10.9m unvested restricted shares, 3.64% of issued shares, against a 2026-08-03 price of NT$610.

The revealed framework: fund the capex customers ask for whatever it costs, pay a dividend sized to roughly 70% of accounting earnings regardless of whether free cash flow supports it, borrow the difference, and use buybacks as an occasional price-support device. Two passages are unusually candid about the absence of a framework. Tien Wu, Q4 2025 call: "There is no guideline. CapEx, Joseph and I, we were very comfortable with $2 billion for the longest time. And then for some reason, we just showed up $4 billion. And then we showed up like $5 billion. And then Joseph talks about even bigger number. I'm not comfortable. I think he is not comfortable. We're all under pressure." And Q2 2026: "ASE is building 13 new facility simultaneously this year. And we just bought another 7 brownfield. So we're building, we're buying, and we're spending CapEx. We're not happy about it. But the question now is that is our obligation. This is why we're here."

One filed statement sits against the call framing. The FY2025 20-F says ASE expects "to meet our payment obligations through the expected cash flow from operations, long-term borrowings, and the issuance of additional equity," and adds that "the issuance of additional equity securities may result in additional dilution to our shareholders." The same filing states that 2026 capex "will be financed through existing cash, expected cash flow from operations, and existing credit lines under our loan facilities", a statement written against a roughly US$7bn plan that is now 50% larger and never updated.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

ASE's record is one very large, expensive, contested acquisition followed by eight years of small, cheap, customer-sourced asset purchases and three well-timed exits. The two halves grade differently and should not be averaged.

SPIL is 81.0% of everything ASE has spent on M&A, NT$168.4bn of the NT$208.0bn on the ledger below and 88.7% of it excluding the 2010 USI tender, and the goodwill impairment test does not measure the deal. The SPIL goodwill of NT$39,990,231 thousand was allocated to the packaging and testing cash-generating units, which is essentially the whole ATM business, so a write-down would require ASE's entire assembly-and-test business to be worth less than its carrying amount. The test that does apply is the margin record: ASE standalone earned an 8.7% operating margin in 2017 with EMS at 46.1% of revenue, and in 2025, with EMS down to 39.9% and the higher-margin ATM mix correspondingly up about six points, the group earned 8.0%. Eight years and roughly NT$160bn of cumulative cash later, consolidated operating margin has not durably exceeded the pre-deal level▪; only 2021 (11.1%) and 2022 (12.1%), both shortage years, cleared it. 4Q25 at 9.9%, 1Q26 at 10.1% and 2Q26 at 11.1% are the first non-shortage quarters above that 8.7% pre-deal margin.

The post-2018 purchases are a different and better business. Since 2019 ASE has bought capacity from its own customers at prices that produced almost no goodwill and, in one case, a gain on bargain purchase; two of them, the Cavite site and the ADI Penang site, carry a long-term supply agreement from the seller. Combined goodwill created by every acquisition closed since 2021 is NT$21,001 thousand against NT$5,359,252 thousand of consideration, 0.4%.

11.2 What the record shows

The SPIL price and how it moved: the opening tender was NT$45 per common share in August 2015; SPIL's board responded that a fair price was NT$48.91–60.58; ASE raised to NT$55 in December 2015 and that offer failed when the Taiwan FTC did not rule before expiry; ASE bought 258.3m shares in the open market instead and finally settled at NT$51.2 in April 2018, inside SPIL's own defence range and below its midpoint (taipeitimes.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web]. ASE paid roughly 2.1x revenue and 1.7x book for a business whose gross margin was 14.9% against ASE's consolidated 18.2% that year. The deal was debt-funded: 2018 financing activities produced a NT$83,111m inflow, and as late as 3Q20 management was still describing a 60–65% net-debt-to-equity deleveraging target.

Synergies were claimed once and then dropped. The ~200bp ATM margin target was met on management's own account in 2020 ("has improved 2.2 to 2.3 percentage points"), attributed to "mainly from SPIL synergy, economies of scale, efficiency improvement as well as technology leadership" without separating the four. The word "synergy" appears in 12 of the 24 archived transcripts, concentrated in 2020–22, and the last substantive SPIL-synergy discussion is 2Q22. No post-2018 acquisition has ever been given a synergy target, a return figure or a deal-specific slide.

The China exit is not as clean as the gain implies. Of the NT$36,939,133 thousand headline, NT$10,533,600 thousand (US$380m) was never paid in cash. It became a 16.48% unlisted minority stake in Hongkong United Ascend Holdings Limited, completed 33 months after the sale, recorded at Level 3 fair value equal to cost with no observable price and no mark since September 2024. ASE separately agreed in March 2023 to buy 19% of UTAC Yantai Co., Ltd. from Hongkong United Ascend for US$5.29m (marketscreener.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web], which is the only external thread on the entity. The archived 20-Fs never describe its business or give Level 3 valuation inputs, so its identification as part of a back-end platform is not established from disclosure.

The goodwill and impairment record: group goodwill was NT$52,541,905 thousand at 2025-12-31 (packaging NT$35,430,752k, testing NT$13,440,470k, EMS NT$3,655,360k, others NT$15,323k). Cumulative goodwill impairment across 2018–2025 is NT$132,778 thousand against roughly NT$47bn of goodwill created, 0.28%, and the 2025 write-off reconciles exactly to the entire AMPI goodwill recognised in 2019. Discount rates used in the value-in-use test declined to 11.96–13.81% in 2025 from 13.91–14.56% in 2024, which mechanically raises recoverable amounts in the year the only post-merger impairment was recorded. The identifiable intangibles the SPIL purchase-price allocation created have amortised from NT$31,354,386 thousand at recognition to a group total of NT$12,920,602 thousand at end-2025: the part of the price that had to be tested against reality has largely been expensed, and the part that does not have to be tested has not moved.

Disciplined buyer of assets, expensive buyer of a company: everything acquired since 2018 totals roughly NT$21.5bn of consideration, about 13% of what SPIL cost and 3.3% of FY2025 revenue, and none of it is advanced packaging: the Infineon and ADI sites are power-module, lead-frame and mature-node back-end capacity, and FAFG, Hirschmann and EugenLight sit in EMS. ASE's advanced-packaging build runs through capex rather than M&A: NT$171,616,529 thousand of PP&E purchases in 2025 alone, 50x the ADI Penang price.

Hirschmann's consideration was restated upward from 2,016,595 to 2,317,201 and its goodwill quadrupled from 5,147 to 21,001 between the FY2023 and FY2025 20-Fs, one of three restatements that make the ledger hard to chart from a single filing. FAFG's consideration was restated downward from 12,829,372 to 12,443,637 with goodwill cut 44.5%, the sign flip on the contingent line being the missed earn-out. And the Infineon contingent consideration is described as revenue-linked but is not: if the target is missed in any of 2025, 2026 or 2027, the corresponding portion is simply paid in 2028, so the contingency is on timing rather than amount.

12. Capitalization and balance sheet

Total interest-bearing debt was NT$213,868m at 2024-12-31, NT$272,945m at 2025-12-31 and NT$306,200m at 2026-06-30, a 43.2% increase in eighteen months, and over the same period operating cash flow did not cover capex once. The CFO has stated the plan: "the funding gap will mostly be funded by additional borrowing" (Q1 2026 call).

Weighted-average cost of debt = principal-weighted stated coupon across the stack excluding leases, with floating legs shown at the reference rate prevailing at the balance-sheet date, which is how the filing presents them.

On that basis the weighted-average coupon is 2.60% (short-term 2.9% on the NT$43,328m of short-term rows, long-term 2.6% on the NT$220,505m of long-term rows). Those eleven rows sum to NT$263,833m excluding leases and NT$272,681m including them, NT$264m below the filing's NT$264,097m and NT$272,945m; the total row above is the filing's figure, not the sum of the rows. The reconstructed floating total of NT$229,241m ties to the disclosed NT$229,258m within 0.007%.

The cash rate is materially higher and it is the one that matters. FY2025 interest paid was NT$7,870m and interest expense NT$7,478m, with NT$668m of borrowing costs capitalised into PP&E, so gross interest incurred was NT$8,146m. On average debt excluding leases of NT$235,077m that is an all-in realised rate of 3.47% and a P&L rate of 3.18%, against the 2.60% spot coupon. The gap is closing because rates on the existing stack came down through 2025 and the incremental money is cheaper still, with the NT$50bn syndicate at 2.06%. Marginal cost of debt is below the average cost of the debt already outstanding. Capitalised borrowing costs went NT$108m (2023) to NT$286m (2024) to NT$668m (2025).

Roughly 45% of the stack is NT$ at 1.26%–2.00%, 31% is US$ at 4.02%–4.29%, 12% is RMB at 1.25%–2.60% and 4% is EUR at 2.03%–3.27%, the four named currencies together 92% of the stack. The expensive US dollar leg exists as a hedge rather than as funding: "Our hedging strategy was to lift borrowings denominated in foreign currencies to avoid exchange rate exposure from its investments in equity instruments denominated in foreign currencies… and net investment in foreign subsidiary, USIFR." Refinancing it into NT$ at the current 1.83% floating rate would save roughly NT$1.7bn of annual interest and give up the hedge.

The 2027 bucket is NT$ floating 47,374; NT$ fixed 3,150; US$ floating 2,496.2m = NT$78,307; RMB floating 1,323; RMB fixed 9,137 (the convertible); EUR fixed 558. Two events since the balance-sheet date have reduced it: the USI Shanghai convertible converted to equity in January 2026, removing NT$9,138m entirely, and ASE early-settled NT$37,399m of bank loans between January and March 2026 whose original settlement dates ran from January 2027 to November 2040. Net of both, the residual 2027 wall is roughly NT$112bn [estimate: NT$139,848m less the conversion less about half the early settlement; range NT$93bn–NT$131bn depending on how much of the early settlement was 2027-dated, which is not disclosed]. Even at the low end that is a single-year refinancing of about 35% of total debt, against NT$396,197m of unused committed credit lines. The largest single instrument is the US$2,496.2m floating facility at 4.02%, which grew from US$1,886.9m a year earlier as ASE pushed a 2026 tranche into 2027 once already.

Floating-rate liabilities grew 51.6% in FY2025 while floating-rate assets were flat, so net exposure grew 74.8%. On the reconstruction, 86.9% of the stack is floating. After the January 2026 conversion and the April 2026 bond maturity, remaining fixed-rate debt is roughly NT$21.8bn plus about NT$13.0bn of bonds issued in 2Q26, against NT$306.2bn of total debt, a fixed share near 11% [estimate]. At 2Q26 debt levels a 100bp move is worth roughly NT$2.4–2.7bn of pre-tax profit. Item 11 of the FY2025 20-F opens with "Interest rate risk was not significant as the cost of capital was expected to be fixed," two paragraphs above the table showing the opposite.

Collateral changed shape in one year. Assets pledged for bank borrowings, tariff guarantees or collateral went from NT$22,556m to NT$52,372m, and within that, pledged property, plant and equipment went from NT$913 thousand to NT$34,209m. Disclosed secured borrowings did not rise to match: secured short-term loans declined from NT$280m to NT$86m and mortgage loans from NT$8,458m to NT$7,886m. The NT$34.2bn of newly pledged PP&E therefore secures either facilities not identified as secured in Note 20 or non-debt obligations, and no disclosure explains it.

12.4 Structural seniority, covenants and liquidity

ASEH is a pure holding company incorporated in 2018. Every operating asset and effectively all the debt sits at subsidiaries: ASE, SPIL, USI Inc., USI Shanghai (71.6%, separately listed), HCC (75.1%), FAFG/Asteelflash, Hirschmann. The covenant disclosure confirms where the credit agreements live: "For certain of the aforementioned revolving bank loans, the subsidiaries are required to maintain specified financial ratios, which are calculated based on annual or semiannual self-prepared financial statements during the loan periods." No metric, no threshold and no headroom is published anywhere, and the tests run on self-prepared statements at annual or semi-annual frequency. Subsidiary lenders sit structurally senior to ASEH-level claims, and non-controlling interests of NT$29,992m at 2Q26 sit ahead of ASEH shareholders where they exist.

The funding model is domestic. NT$396,197m of undrawn committed lines against NT$306,200m of drawn debt means ASE can fund a full year of guided capex from committed capacity without touching a public market. ASE has no S&P and no Moody's rating despite an US$81bn market capitalisation and an NYSE listing; only Fitch rates it, at BBB / Stable. Domestic bonds outstanding total NT$5.5bn at coupons of 0.95%–1.03%, an order of magnitude smaller than the bank stack.

Leases and pension: right-of-use assets were NT$12,637m at 2025-12-31 and NT$13,996m at 2026-06-30, mostly land and buildings; machinery right-of-use assets declined from NT$546m to NT$215m. Meanwhile expenses for short-term leases, which create no lease liability under the IFRS 16 exemption, went NT$317m (2023) to NT$886m (2024) to NT$1,660m (2025), a 5.2x increase in two years. Capitalising that at a three-year effective term and the 2.6% weighted cost adds roughly NT$4.7bn of debt-like obligation [estimate], small against NT$264bn but invisible in reported leverage. Separately, testers consigned by customers never appear as ASE assets at all, so reported capex understates the capacity being installed. Pension is immaterial: a NT$4,002m net obligation, 68.4% funded, 1.1% of total equity.

The 2018 acquisition levered the balance sheet (net debt/EBITDA 0.57x to 2.11x in one year, peaking at 2.18x in 2019), three years of deleveraging followed to 1.06x by 2022, and the direction reversed in 2025 when financing activities swung to a NT$45,269m inflow, the first since 2018. Against Amkor, the only direct OSAT comparable and a company funding a similar advanced-packaging build, ASE runs 70.6% total debt to equity against 34.6% and, on Bloomberg's trailing basis for both companies, 1.17x net debt/EBITDA against 0.06x; the 1.28x above is the same ratio computed on §12's own debt definition at 2Q26. The ratings run the other way: ASE is investment grade at Fitch BBB, Amkor is high yield at BB+/BB/Ba2. The gap reflects scale and the Taiwanese bank relationship base rather than the arithmetic of the balance sheet.

Net dilution runs 0.7–1.0% a year with no buyback to offset it.

12.6 Structural balance-sheet risks

  1. The 2027 refinancing concentration. 63.4% of long-term debt in one calendar year, reduced to NT$93bn–NT$131bn, roughly NT$112bn at the midpoint [estimate], by the January conversion and the first-quarter early settlements, with a US$2,496m floating facility as the largest single piece. Leading indicator: whether the 2027 bucket in the FY2026 20-F has been termed out or has grown again.
  2. An essentially unhedged floating book on a debt stack scaling toward NT$400bn. 86.9% floating, disclosed 100bp sensitivity of NT$1,833m rising toward NT$2.4–2.7bn. Item 5 says ASE has "sometimes" entered interest-rate swaps; no swap notional appears in the FY2025 disclosures, only FX forwards and swaps.
  3. Permanent debt against cyclical EBITDA with a fixed depreciation step-up behind it. Adding roughly NT$500bn of gross PP&E across FY2025–FY2026 at ASE's realised asset lives pushes D&A toward NT$140–170bn a year [estimate: incremental additions at an implied blended life of 5–7 years derived from FY2025 D&A on gross PP&E], a level §17.1's roll-forward reaches between FY2029 and FY2032 rather than by 2028. At a FY2023-style trough with NT$400bn of debt, net debt/EBITDA would be roughly 3.1x and operating income at or below zero once the higher depreciation ran through. This is the mechanism by which the balance sheet breaks.
  4. Undisclosed covenants at undisclosed subsidiaries, tested on self-prepared statements. Leading indicator: any change to the compliance sentence in Note 20c, or a waiver disclosure.
  5. New encumbrance without a matching disclosed liability. NT$34,209m of newly pledged PP&E against NT$7,972m of disclosed secured borrowings, a 4.3x over-collateralisation with no explanation.
  6. Structural subordination of the holding company, with material outside shareholders at three subsidiaries and NCI growing from NT$22,245m to NT$29,992m in eighteen months.
  7. Persistent, accelerating dilution with no buyback, and a 3.64% option and restricted-stock overhang.
  8. An FX mismatch that is partly deliberate, where the most expensive tranche cannot be refinanced into cheap NT$ without giving up the hedge it exists to provide.
  9. Off-balance-sheet equipment leases growing 5.2x in two years, worth roughly NT$4.7bn of unrecognised obligation [estimate].

12.7 Where the funding goes from here

FY2026 capex is guided at about US$10.5bn, roughly NT$331bn at NT$31.5. Applying the FY2025 cash-conversion ratio of 96% (NT$164,643m of cash capex on NT$171,617m of accrual capex) gives about NT$317bn of cash capex; assuming FY2026 operating cash flow of NT$195–200bn and adding the NT$29.4bn dividend, the FY2026 external funding need is NT$146–151bn [estimate: method as stated; bounds NT$370bn to NT$440bn of year-end debt depending on capex timing and whether the unexplained non-debt inflow repeats]. On NT$272.9bn of debt at 2025-12-31 that implies year-end 2026 debt near NT$420bn, against the NT$428,110m §17.1 carries. At that year-end level and a 2.8% weighted cost, annual interest would be roughly NT$11–12bn against NT$7,478m in FY2025 and against the model's NT$9,998m, which is struck on average rather than year-end debt. Interest coverage would be 6.4x–7.0x on the 1H26 operating run-rate of NT$77,254m annualised.

The depreciation consequence is larger than the interest consequence, and one liability line could change the whole framing. Other non-current liabilities went NT$5,825m (2023) to NT$7,057m (2024) to NT$37,585m (2025), and on the 6-K basis to NT$90,750m by 2Q26, with no line-item breakdown in the 20-F. The only candidates the filing identifies are customer advance payments under long-term agreements and IAS 20 asset-related government grants recognised as deferred revenue. If it is customer prepayment, a material share of the LEAP build is being pre-funded interest-free by customers and the capacity is contracted; if it is grants, it is a subsidy releasing into other income over the assets' lives. The two have opposite implications for the durability of the revenue, and management has never mentioned the line on any call.

What changed: six of the eight headline metrics inflected in the last two quarters and all in the same direction. Revenue growth went from +8.4% for FY2025 to +26.7% in 2Q26. Consolidated gross margin is 3.3 points above the year and operating margin 3.1 points above it, the highest since FY2022. Testers rose 13.4% in two quarters. Equipment capex roughly doubled per quarter. Free cash flow deteriorated to −NT$40,540m across 1H26, already 1.8x the whole FY2025 deficit. Management's own account on the 2Q26 call: "second quarter ATM revenues came in ahead of our original expectations driven by higher loading from both our LEAP and general services… we also saw our gross margin outpacing our original expectations, driven by higher loading, resulting in more operating leverage," with the constraint now on the supply side: "Our capability for near-term incremental growth is being gated by our abilities to install capital equipment and build out our buildings and facilities."

The two exceptions run the other way. EMS gross margin of 8.9% in 2Q26 is below the FY2025 figure and its operating margin of 2.4% is the lowest of the ten quarters on record, attributed by management principally to product mix and a higher component-cost environment. And the wire bonder count is down 4.0% from the FY2022 peak, in line with its multi-year trend.

13.3 What drove the record

FY2024 to FY2025, gross margin 16.3% to 17.7%: from the 20-F Item 5 cost ratios: raw materials 51.5% to 48.4% of operating revenues, a 3.1-point favourable move driven by the mix shift from EMS to ATM; labour 10.8% to 11.3%, adverse on headcount added in packaging; depreciation, amortization and rental in operating costs 9.1% to 9.6%, adverse as new capacity began to depreciate; and other operating costs 12.3% to 13.0%, adverse on utilities. Management attributes the gain to "higher packaging and testing revenue mix and higher factory utilization of our packaging and testing equipment, offset in part by the appreciating NT dollars and higher utility costs."

FY2024 to FY2025, operating margin 6.8% to 8.0%: gross margin +1.4pp, operating expenses 9.70% to 9.83% of revenue (R&D alone 4.84% to 5.09%), other operating income 0.20% to 0.10%.

FY2023 to FY2024, the year margins went backwards: gross margin rose 15.8% to 16.3% while operating margin declined 7.2% to 6.8%, because operating expenses rose from 8.84% to 9.70% of revenue and R&D from 4.38% to 4.84%. ASE kept spending on leading-edge development through a year in which revenue barely moved.

FY2022 to FY2023, the downcycle: revenue −13.3%, gross margin −4.3pp, operating margin −4.9pp. Decremental operating margin of 44.4%. That is the operating leverage of the business running in reverse.

Incremental margin on the way up: 15.4% from FY2023 to FY2025, 22.2% in FY2025 alone and 28.5% in 1H26 against 1H25. The incremental margin is climbing as the mix shifts to ATM and remains below the 44.4% decremental rate.

Purchase-price-allocation drag: SPIL PPA added NT$4,194m of expense in 2024 and NT$2,956m in 2025. Excluding all PPA, management reported FY2025 gross margin of 18% and operating margin of 8.4% against reported 17.7% and 8.0%. Intangibles ex-goodwill have amortised from NT$30,898m at FY2018 year-end, against the NT$31,354m recognised in the SPIL purchase-price allocation itself, to NT$12,921m (FY2025), so the drag shrinks by roughly NT$1bn a year on its own.

Cash conversion: FCF/EBITDA has been at or below 0.3x in seven of the ten years, and the two strong years (FY2016 at 0.5x, FY2023 at 0.6x) were both years in which capex was cut. This is a business whose cash generation is a function of whether it is building rather than of its margins. Working capital is stable and mildly favourable: the cash conversion cycle sat between 42.6 and 68.1 days across ten years and was 54.9 days in FY2025, essentially unchanged from FY2023's 54.5. The capital intensity is all fixed assets.

The inflections these reveal: the tester fleet grew 32.5% in six quarters while the wire bonder fleet declined 2.0%, which is the mix shift stated in physical units. Revenue per tester rose 13.7% over the same span and then went flat for three quarters while the fleet grew 13.4%, which is the point at which test growth switched from price-and-loading-led to capacity-led. Substrate self-supply, ASE's own hedge against the constraint it names, is 8.7% against 29.7% a decade ago. SMT lines have been cut 10.9% from the January 2023 peak while EMS gross profit per line rose 13.6% against FY2023, which is consolidation leverage rather than volume leverage. And the top-five customer percentage improves on a group basis while worsening on the ATM basis, because the group figure is flattered by EMS shrinking.

14. Expectations: internal against external against base rates

The headline disagreement is not about revenue and not about FY2026. It is that consensus requires a full-year ATM gross margin of roughly 30.6% in FY2027 and 32.4% in FY2028, above the top of a range management has touched in one quarter four years ago and has twice declined to raise, on a utilization map management published itself that puts 30% at full capacity.▪

14.1 The internal record

ASE guides one quarter forward only and has never given full-year revenue, EPS or margin guidance in any of the twenty-four calls in the archive.

ASE systematically under-guides its semiconductor business and guides EMS roughly straight.▪ The ATM lines beat 71–79% of the time and missed once in six years; the EMS lines beat 38–46% and account for six of the eight total misses. The bias has widened rather than tightened: in the numeric-range era the ATM gross margin has come in 30–370bp above the top of its guided band in four consecutive quarters, and consolidated revenue has beaten the top of its band by 1.0–5.8 points in all four quarters that line has existed.

The one material miss in six years, 2Q25, was currency. Guidance set in April 2025 was overtaken by the NT dollar's appreciation in early May; management quantified the damage precisely the following quarter and has not given a comparable bridge in the beat direction, while the assumed rate moved from 29.2 for 3Q25 to 31.9 for 3Q26.

14.2 The external record

The rating distribution on the Taiwan line, 24 buy and 1 hold with no sell, suggests more agreement than there is: the target distribution runs NT$545 to NT$840, a 54% spread, against a spot of NT$610. Three analysts rated buy or outperform publish targets below the spot price, including Daiwa and Macquarie, both dated after the 2Q26 print. The NYSE ADR line shows three recommendations and two contributing EPS estimates against twenty-five and twenty-two locally, so anyone reading US-sourced consensus for this company is reading a two-analyst panel.

The upgrade is ten months old and it is a margin upgrade. From the September-2025 trough, FY2026 revenue consensus is up 18.7% while FY2026 EPS consensus is up 59.4%; for FY2027, revenue +31.9% and EPS +87.8%. Against peers, on the longer window Bloomberg's revision series supports — January 2025 to date — ASE has the smallest FY2027 revenue upgrade of the Taiwan set (+25.5% against TSMC +44.6%, King Yuan +46.8%, Powertech +36.7%) and the largest FY2027 EPS upgrade (+74.1%, ahead even of TSMC's +68.9%). Its EPS-to-revenue upgrade ratio of 2.91x is the highest of any peer with a credible estimate panel. Amkor is the control: +6.4% on FY2026 EPS and +11.1% on FY2027, and the only name in the group where the revenue upgrade exceeds the EPS upgrade.

Dispersion is in earnings rather than revenue and widens with horizon. FY2026 EPS coefficient of variation is 5.9% on 22 estimates, FY2027 9.9% on 21, FY2028 13.8% on 12. The FY2028 low estimate of NT$26.28 is below the FY2027 mean of NT$28.04, so at least one analyst models earnings going sideways or down from 2027 to 2028. Only 12 of 25 analysts publish an FY2028 number at all, and the outer year is where the lowest forward multiples come from.

For the next quarter there is no cushion. Consensus 3Q26 revenue of NT$233,027m sits within 0.05% of the top of management's guided range of NT$231,231–233,142m, and consensus gross margin of 21.15% sits in the upper half of the guided 20.5–21.5%.

14.3 What the outside view says

The reference class is eight OSATs across FY2009–FY2025, 126 company-years of gross margin and 123 of ROIC, plus a wider capital-intensive semiconductor class for the capex questions and four US-listed contract manufacturers for EMS.

Growth does not persist: forward three-year revenue CAGR is nearly flat across starting conditions, and consecutive 20%+ years occurred six times in 118 company-years with only three runs of three or more, every one of them from a revenue base below US$1.5bn. Next, heavy capex buys revenue and not returns: across 39 OSAT capex-surge events with a three-year outcome, ROIC was higher three years later in 15 cases (38%), the median change was −0.8 points, and the median revenue CAGR over the following three years was +14.7%▪. And above-trend margins give back about two points over three years: across 31 observations, the median change in gross margin three years after an above-trend year is −2.0 points, and ASE's own local proof is harsher, with ATM-basis gross margin going from 28.7% to 22.2% in one year between FY2022 and FY2023.

The one demanding assumption the record supports is capital productivity. ASE's own median of 0.78 of incremental revenue per unit of three-year capex is the best in its reference class by a wide margin, against a class median of 0.37, and consensus implies 0.73.▪ The assumption with no precedent in the class is the 30%-plus ATM gross margin.

Two consensus revenue sets for FY2026 came off the same terminal on the same date: NT$837,332m and NT$958,499m. Only the first reconciles with management's own 3Q26 guide; reaching the higher figure would require 4Q26 revenue about 56% above 3Q26. The comparisons above use NT$837,332m and the ratio-based placements are unaffected.

FY2025 LEAP landed at US$1.6bn and 13% of ATM revenue, testing grew 36%, and 2026 LEAP was guided to "double from USD 1.6 billion to USD 3.2 billion," with ATM gross margin expected to stay inside the 24–30% range "throughout the year and to improve every quarter"
2Q26, 2026-07-30 ADR +11.7%, but only +3.5pp against the SOX, which rose 8.2% that session while Amkor rose 12.9% Most of the eleven-point move was the sector rebounding out of the July correction. The company-specific increment came from ATM gross margin of 27.3% ahead of guidance, net profit of NT$21.1bn (+180% YoY), ATM at 66% of revenue but 94% of operating profit, LEAP tracking ahead of US$3.5bn with a 2027 doubling targeted, the general segment raised to +20% from +13%, and 4Q26 ATM gross margin "likely to exceed our structural margin ceiling of 30%." Against that, 2026 capex was raised US$2bn to US$10.5bn
2Q24, 2024-07-25 ADR −2.3%; TWSE −9.9% next session A +13.8% EPS beat with a limit-down local reaction, and none of it was ASE. The print landed inside the July–August 2024 global semiconductor drawdown; ASE's release-day move was −0.3pp against the SOX

2015–2020, the flat decade: consensus 12-month forward EPS sat in the NT$5–6 range for the whole span. ASE was a wire-bond-weighted commodity assembler through the smartphone plateau, and the 2018 holdco with SPIL added scale rather than mix. The FY2019 20-F records net profit attributable declining 34.9% to NT$17,061m on trade-war and smartphone destocking.

2021–2022, a pure multiple event: earnings did not decline. FY2022 diluted EPS per ADS of NT$27.61 was a record at the time. The forward multiple went from 9.0x to a series low of 6.0x on 2022-06-30. The market priced a coming inventory correction and got it, with FY2023 EPS per ADS at NT$16.08, −42%.

2022–2024, the first AI re-rating, entirely multiple: forward EPS was flat to down across the window while the forward P/E went 6.0x to about 15.5x. On the 4Q24 call management first quantified the driver.

2024–2025, the tariff drawdown: the decline was market-wide in April 2025, with an ASE-specific overlay. The NT dollar moved from an average of 32.8 to 31.2 within the second quarter, and management's own sensitivity is "for every percentage point appreciation of the NT dollar… a 0.3 percentage point negative impact to our gross and operating margins at the holding company level and a 0.45 percentage point negative impact… at the ATM level."

2025–2026, the LEAP inflection: consensus EPS was beaten by +24.3%, +20.0%, +16.2% and +26.3% in four consecutive quarters, and guidance was raised at every one.

June–July 2026, a 31% drawdown in one month: the ADR declined from US$45.12 (2026-06-30) to US$31.12 (2026-07-29). Over the same window TSMC reported 2Q26 on 2026-07-16 with 2026 capex guided to US$60–64bn against a prior US$52–56bn; on 2026-07-17 the TAIEX declined 2,953.71 points, or 6.47%, with foreign institutions net sellers of NT$189.04bn (taipeitimes.com, accessed 2026-08-03) [web], and the SOX ended that week more than 20% below its late-June high. ASE's daily moves tracked the SOX closely through the window: −6.6% against −4.3% on 7/24, −7.2% against −4.5% on 7/28, −8.3% against −5.3% on 7/29. The decline was sector-wide; whether the TSMC capex guide caused it is not established by the price series alone.

Through the post-COVID upcycle the forward multiple was cut from 10.9x to 6.0x while forward EPS more than doubled between end-2018 and mid-2022, and the price added 31%. Between mid-2022 and September 2025 the entire 115% gain was re-rating, with forward consensus EPS lower at the end of the window than at the start. Only from October 2025 do earnings and multiple move together, and even then the multiple contributed a third. Over the whole eight-and-a-half-year span, in log terms, earnings account for about 64% of the price change and the multiple about 36%.
